speechtext:
I am pleased to announce that the date of the unveiling of the Macphail memorial has been fixed by the internal economy commission for Tuesday, March 8, 1955. It was on March 8, 1922, that the late Agnes Campbell Macphail, elected member for the constituency of Grey Southeast at the general elections held on December 6, 1921, took her seat in the house, the first woman to do so.
Hon. members will recall that on June 8, 1954, I communicated the recommendations of the commissioners of internal economy which were as follows: (a) that to commemorate this historic event, a bronze bust of the first woman member, Miss Agnes Macphail, be placed on a pedestal in the vicinity of the chamber of the House of Commons; and (b) that, for this purpose, the bronze bust of Miss Macphail, offered by her two sisters, be gratefully accepted.
On Tuesday, March 8 next, it is proposed to adjourn the house at five p.m. Hon. senators and members are invited to gather in this chamber at 5.30 p.m. to hear the tributes which will be paid to the late Miss Macphail. Miss Macphail's close relatives have been invited to attend the ceremony on the floor of the house.
When the speeches are concluded, Mrs. Meredith Reany and Mrs. Hugh Bailey, sisters
of Miss Macphail, will proceed to the southwest corridor to declare the Macphail memorial officially unveiled.
The public is cordially invited to attend.

subtopic: DETENTION OF DEPORTEES IN TORONTO JAIL
speechtext:
On Friday last, the hon. member for York South asked me on the orders of the day whether it was a fact that immigrants ordered to be deported are sometimes held in Toronto jail for more than a month at a cost of $10 a day to Canadian taxpayers, even though they offer to pay their own way back to their country of origin and to leave as soon as they are notified of deportation action. So far as I can discover, this is not a fact.
In the first place, the cost of detention is not $10 a day but $3 a day. In the second place, after a review of all cases of persons detained for 30 days or more during the years 1951 to 1954 inclusive, only one case has been found of a person who volunteered to leave this country of his own accord, and the privilege of leaving voluntarily was denied to this person because he could not establish that he had the means to provide for his transportation to Europe.
After asking his question, the hon. member sent me a letter on which his question had been founded. This letter was from a Dutch immigrant whose name I would prefer not to give to the house. This immigrant had been convicted on two occasions of theft and on both occasions had, perhaps mistakenly, been allowed to remain in this country on compassionate grounds. His wife subsequently reported that he had deserted her and their children and, as there was no evidence that he intended to return to his wife and support his family or that he had been rehabilitated in any way, this immigrant was apprehended on January 24, 1955, and immediate steps were taken to arrange with The Netherlands authorities for his deportation. It took some time to secure the necessary permission, which has now been received, and as his deportation is imminent he is being removed to detention headquarters in Montreal pending actual deportation.
I might add that the department has no record of any offer by this immigrant to depart voluntarily and, in any event, we

Concerning the matter of courtesy, I was not referring to the hon. member for Hamilton West but I think the procedure might be accepted by the member of the official opposition in this particular instance because we endeavoured to initiate the debate first.

Mr. Speaker, I think I will deal first of all with what has happened, and say to hon. members that I am sure they will agree with me when I say that since I have been a member of the house I have neither asked nor given quarter in debate, because of my sex. And I rather resent the inference of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that it was because of that I had risen to take part in this debate.
I am here as a member of the House of Commons with certain duties to perform, speaking for my party on matters arising which are of special interest to labour; and I propose to exercise my duty in the best manner available to me. Those members of the House of Commons who desire to cast aspersions on the manner in which I do it are at liberty to do so-but that will not deter me at any time from doing what I consider it is my duty to do.
Then, with regard to the matter which has been raised and which, as my leader pointed out, we had intended to raise in this manner, I must say that members of this party had considered the possibility of asking for the adjournment of the house, as was done last Thursday. However, we do know that a debate instigated in that manner would die with that sitting. Accordingly we thought that, for the purpose of having a fuller and more extended debate on a subject which is of such vital concern to the people of this country, we should proceed in this more regularized manner to present our views to the house and the government. It is also true, Mr. Speaker, that had the debate died with the sitting there would have been no opportunity for collecting the voices in this matter. That also influenced us in our decision to wait.
There are many aspects to this problem of unemployment. First of all of course there is the annual squabble which takes place over which are the right figures, as to how many people are actually unemployed. Then there is the question of the number who are receiving unemployment insurance benefits and the impact which that has on the welfare load which falls, in the main, upon the municipalities, which have only one source of revenue. That, in turn, leads us to the over-all question of what happens to the

economy of Canada under circumstances like this; and that in turn leads us to the question of what is to be done about it.
I should like first of all to deal with the question of the numbers of people who are unemployed in this country. I have made a considerable study of this matter and have called upon others to assist me in securing the best possible information we could secure on the situation today.
It is true that there has been a deterioration in the employment picture all through 1954. The latest figures available, for January 1955, of applications on file at national employment offices total 569,600 or an increase of 206,900 over last year-an increase, let me say, of 57 per cent.
Throughout the whole of 1954, I reiterate, there has been a marked deterioration in the employment situation. Comments have been made each year to the effect that when winter broke and spring came many of our problems would be cleared up. So, with this in mind, I looked at the spring and summer months of 1953 and 1954, extending my survey into the autumn. I found that in the months of May to October 1953 inclusive- and certainly neither May nor October could be called a winter month-the percentage of applications for employment to the total civilian labour force ranged from 3 per cent in the mid-summer months to 4-2 per cent. Those figures when compared with the figures for 1954 show that in 1954 the percentage of applications for employment to the total civilian labour force ranged from 4-4 per cent to 6-6 per cent, or an increase of at least 50 per cent between 1953 and 1954.
This deterioration can be seen from the fact that at all national employment service offices in every single month the total number of people in the civilian labour force has been higher than in the corresponding month of the previous year. For example, applications for employment in January 1955 are 10 [DOT] 7 per cent as against the corresponding figure of 10 per cent in January of 1954. The sorry part of it is that if the increase in the number of applications for work in March of this year, the month into which we just entered today, bear the same relationship to the January figures for 1955 that the March figures bear to the January figures in 1954, there will be 620,000 unplaced applicants in Canada during the course of this present month. That will represent 11'6 per cent of the present labour force, as against 10-9 per cent applying for jobs last year.
From time to time government speakers have maintained that the national employment service figures overstate the condition

of unemployment. They have claimed that not all applicants for employment are necessarily out of work, or are regularly part of the labour force. However, evidence of the deterioration in the employment situation is equally strong if we analyse the figures from the sample survey of the labour force taken by the dominion bureau of statistics.
For this purpose I have secured the percentages of unemployed, according to the D.B.S. figures, which is the other set of figures from which we glean information on the subject. Upon doing this I find that in 1953 the D.B.S. figures showed a percentage of unemployed ranging from 1-6 per cent to 3-6 per cent, while the figures from the same source show for 1954 percentages of unemployment ranging from 3 per cent to 6 per cent-again twice as much, practically, as the year before.
I find also from these figures, which government spokesmen are fond of quoting as against the higher figures of the national employment service, that in January 1955, the last month for which figures are available, even the dominion bureau of statistics showed 6-8 per cent unemployed, which is 1-5 per cent higher than the figure for the preceding January.
From these figures it is also clear that in every month of 1954 the percentage of unemployed was higher than in the corresponding month of 1953. That situation is getting progressively worse, as shown by the fact that the percentage of labour force unemployed in January 1955 was 6-8 per cent, as I indicated, as against 5-3 per cent in January 1954, and as against 3-6 per cent in January 1953. According to this sample, the actual number of persons without jobs and seeking work in January, 1955, was 362,000, as compared with 569,600 in the national employment service figures.
I realize that without a lengthy study it would be impossible to reconcile these conflicting figures; but it is true that both sets of figures show the same situation, namely, a deterioration in the employment position during 1954 and, according to the latest figures that are available to us, right up to 1955. It is not only the actual figures of unemployment that cause us concern. From the Canadian statistical review, January, 1955, I find that the retail trade of this country has suffered in the last three years. In November, 1952, the retail trade in millions of dollars was 1,006-9. The following year, November, 1953, it was 1,001-7, or a reduction of $5,225,000. The following year, November, 1954, the amount was 994-3, which represented a drop of $7,500,000. We find that
Unemployment
the retail trade gradually dropped while the ordinary claims on the unemployment register gradually rose from November, 1952,-the same months-to 161,900; November, 1953, to 238,500; November, 1954, to 274,500. From the same publication I find on page 12 in the statistics with reference to the civilian labour force, between January, 1953 and January, 1955, there was an increase in the labour force of 145,000. At January, 1953, there were 5,200,000 in the civilian labour force of Canada. In 1955 there were 5,345,000. Without jobs and seeking work in those same months we find the following figures: In January, 1953, 187,000; in 1954, 280,000; and in 1955, 362,000, which gives us an increase of persons without jobs and seeking work in that two-year period of 175,000. At the same time that the total civilian labour force increased by only 145,000, the increase in the number of persons without jobs and seeking work in that two-year period rose by 30,000 over and above the actual increase in the size of the labour force.
This, Mr. Speaker, is cause for grave concern to everyone. But, regardless of the number of people who are out of work, regardless of whether the number is 362,000 or 569,000, the question we have to ask ourselves is whether or not hon. members and the people of Canada are going to consider that a person is merely a statistic. Is the individual to be merely a statistic in the estimation of those people who are governing this country? Each of these 569,000 persons reported by the Department of Labour and each of those reported by the dominion bureau of statistics is a human being. Many of them have persons dependent upon them for support. It is not only a matter of buoyancy or lack of buoyancy of the Canadian economy; it is a matter of frightened men and women with cold bodies and hungry stomachs. It is a matter of fear which grips the hearts of working people who are probably employed themselves but see their neighbours idle and who ask themselves: when is it going to happen to me? Certainly, they say, we expect Canada to go ahead. Certain it is that Canada will thrive, but in the meantime what do we eat?
Not long ago I noticed an article in one of the newspapers with reference to a plea which had been made to the municipal authorities on behalf of the unemployed persons, and it was headed: "Can't Eat Snow". No, Mr. Speaker, they cannot eat snow and they cannot eat Kitimat. They cannot eat Knob Lake; they cannot eat Alberta oil; they cannot eat a pipe line and they cannot eat the St. Lawrence seaway, important though these things are to Canada, and despite the

Unemployment
fact that they supply jobs to large numbers of Canadians. Perhaps that is why this situation is so appalling.
In the midst of wealth we have human misery. The very presence of this wealth, the very picture of progress points up more vividly the lack of constructive planning which results in this actually increasing unemployment problem. With all the faith in the world, Mr. Speaker, these people cannot wait ten years or fifteen years for a steady job and a weekly pay cheque.
We should probably ask ourselves what the government's reaction has been to this. Not so long ago a year-end review by the Minister of Labour was released. Quite frankly, I read it with amazement. It is true that when unemployment is rising the talk of the department is that it is seasonal or regional. When unemployment fell off a bit, the department was prone to describe the situation as encouraging. However, I was not prepared for some of the remarks in this news release. In the very first paragraph the minister remarked that there was some improvement in the level of economic activity and employment, while unemployment continued on a higher level in 1954 than in 1953. Now, I am not very good at this double talk myself, or maybe I am misreading this particular paragraph, Mr. Speaker, but it seems to me when one says that there was some improvement in the level of economic activity and employment and then turns around and says in the same sentence, without a comma in between, that unemployment continued on a higher level, if that is not double talk, I have not read any. As a matter of fact, the article goes on in that vein and I could quote several such instances in it.
Another thing that I should like to mention appears several paragraphs down the page. Reference is made to the relative improvement in the employment picture and the demands for labour which have been sufficiently strong in recent months to reduce the year-to-year gap in the unemployment level. Well, in December, 1954,	352,000
persons were out of work as against 303,000 in 1953, or an increase of 49,000 persons out of work. Is this a relative improvement? If so, relative to what? What does it mean to say that the year-to-year gap in the unemployment level has been reduced?
A couple of paragraphs later it goes on to say that there is a stronger over-all picture employmentwise than was the case a year ago. We might ask ourselves just what this

stronger picture is. In December 1953 the civilian labour force was 5,275,000, and the out of work numbered 303,000 or 5-7 per cent. One year later, in December 1954, at the time this news release was issued, the civilian labour force numbered 5,414,000 and the number out of work was 352.000 or 6-5 per cent, an increase of -8 per cent despite the fact that this release says that there is a stronger over-all picture employmentwise.
A little later on in the release it says that job opportunities should be somewhat more numerous this winter than a year ago. Even at the time of writing this, the minister must have known that unemployment was rising even over the large figure of the previous year. To my mind, while the rest of this might very well be considered double talk, while it might be conceded that the department was trying to put a brave face on what was a very bad situation, the final blow comes in the last paragraph. I almost hesitate to read it for it is no longer double talk, it is flippancy. It says:
Finally I would like to say on behalf of the federal government that you have our best wishes for a happy, successful and productive new year.
A little later on, not so long after this report came out, we had the speech from the throne at the opening of this session-a speech which was full of vagaries and half promises, a speech which said in one place that there was some unemployment of a regional and seasonal nature and in another place that there should be a substantial increase in public works of a sort that will relieve unemployment.
There were some speeches made during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Among those who spoke was the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). It was interesting to note that the Prime Minister had changed his tone a little since September of 1954 when he spoke in the province of Quebec. Among the remarks which he is credited with having made at that time is a sentence which I should like to quote now. According to a Canadian Press dispatch the Prime Minister had this to say:
We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody we are incompetent.
After this house had opened and during the debate on the speech from the throne the Prime Minister, after expressing anxiety about unemployment, had this to say:
Each year the situation has eased as the season advances. There is reason to expect that it will do so again.

I ask: what reason and to what extent? Is it to the extent, to quote the Prime Minister, that there is work for everybody or merely to the extent that the government can alibi itself out of its incompetency? Those words of the Prime Minister did not go unnoticed. In a publication which comes to all of us entitled Labour Research and published by the research department of the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Prime Minister is quoted as having said, which he did, that there is some unemployment in Canada. This article starts out by saying that this classic understatement almost deserves to rank with President Wilson's description of the great war. I am sure that hon. members of this house are familiar with that classic understatement. Then the article goes on to say:
This is really sublime. There has indeed "been some unemployment in Canada every year".
Canadian Business, the official organ of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in December estimated that this year's March figure for unplaced applicants would be around 600,000. The present indication is that it may be higher than that. Last year it was 570,000; in 1953 it was 408,000; in 1952 it was 382,000; and in 1951 it was 296,000. Four years ago it was less than 300,000; this year it is over 600,000. Four years ago about one in thirteen workers unemployed; this year about one in seven. This very remarkable breakdown of employment conditions in Canada goes on to give facts and comparisons of figures which are really amazing.
In the midst of all this many representations have been made, not the least of which was a very fine letter from the Ontario welfare council. Since this is addressed to the right hon. Prime Minister I know he must have received it, and since I received a copy I presume that every hon. member did also. In this letter they set out a most excellent description of the situation.
They point out that there is only some 62 per cent of the labour force which is insured under the Unemployment Insurance Act. They point out also that with some 62 per cent insured there is left a sizeable percentage who cannot hope to benefit even when they are out of work. Then they go on to point out some other things. They say that in addition there are those persons whose benefits have expired. They say also that it is apparent at a time when the employment situation is worsening steadily every year that there are many people in this province who have used up their rights to benefits and have passed from under the protection of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Unemployment
They go on to point out that there are also those persons who are without sufficient credits to claim insurance benefits and that there are also those young people who are entering the labour market, newcomers to Canada and others who are unprotected because they have not worked long enough to earn rights to benefits. They regret further that the benefits are not sufficient to support these people and their families at a minimum subsistence level. Then they make this statement:
It is self-evident that we have a problem whose solution requires federal participation on a major scale-and quickly.
The Ontario welfare council is not the only organization that is concerned in this matter. Briefs have been presented to the government and delegations have come here to meet, not only the government but the opposition parties as well. Across this country newspapers have recorded these things, have written articles and editorials on the subject. I have already mentioned one article which I had seen and which is headed "Can't Eat Snow". It then went on to say that immediate talks were sought on the growing lack of jobs. Another one is headed, "Tomorrow may be Too Late; Help Needed Now for City's Jobless". The next one says that aldermen in one city blast government inaction. Today I received a telegram from the Hamilton council of community services in which it is said:
Public assistance still urgently needed in Hamilton, 14,000 now unemployed. Seventeen thousand spent by city in January and nearly that much in February for unemployed employables without benefits and needing emergency relief. Please urge federal action toward adequate financial assistance program . . .
Another article is headed "Unemployment Mask," and this one proceeds to set out the picture as it is seen by the editorial writers across this country of a progressively worsening situation. The next one says, "Federal Ontario Officials Discuss Job Lack Planning". Then it says that nothing has yet been done with regard to unemployed employables. Again another one is headed "How Many Jobless?" That is a question that we all ask ourselves. Another one is headed, "The Wrong Doorstep" and it sets out the manner this problem has been juggled around from one authority to another, with no one taking any credit for it. Another one is headed, "Jobless Paid to Quit City and Go Home". All of these articles, Mr. Speaker, give evidence of the concern which is felt not only by people in public life, not only by the unemployed themselves but by newspaper writers and newspaper editors throughout this land.

Unemployment
Again I should like to refer to the submission of the Ontario welfare council and its strong plea for consideration. In a closing paragraph of their letter, speaking of the meeting which they had called, they have this to say:
It was clear that those who attended our meeting did not accept general statements that this problem represents no responsibility of the federal government. Since employment-and unemployment-are a national concern, it is self-evident that the fate of unemployed employables is similarly basically sensitive to federal initiative.
And further on it points out what should be a warning to all of us:
. . . the suffering endured by many now will be reflected inevitably in reduced morale, health, productivity and purchasing power of our people.
That, Mr. Speaker, leads directly to the $64 question: Whither the Canadian economy?
This government never displayed any bashfulness at all in accepting credit for boom years. These ministers went up and down the land beating their chests and bragging. They even forgot to give credit to the poor taxpayers who provided the money to pay for the services they bragged about. To hear them tell it, you would think they had dug into their own pockets and paid for them. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, anyone who wants to read the newspapers over the last few years will be surprised to find the number of instances in which ministers of the crown referred to "I" and "we" in their recounting of the events which had taken place. But now, when the municipalities are caught in a giant squeeze, this government will not even admit the desirability of drawing together all levels of public administration to discuss the best means of alleviating the municipal distress, because that is where the big load inevitably falls. It falls right on the municipality with its one source of tax revenue. Having taken credit for the employment boom of a few years ago, surely the government can hardly disclaim responsibility now when unemployment rears its ugly head higher and higher as the years go by.
What has the government done? It has done this, Mr. Speaker. It has published a little pamphlet which is called "Two Minutes of Employment Facts". This pamphlet came into my office postmarked February 9, 1955. It points out that everyone is concerned about the unemployment situation and then it goes on to say this:
Though extremely complex in all Its ramifications, the problem of seasonal unemployment does appear to offer some weak points for immediate attack where there is a reasonable chance for definite progress. Recent extensive studies of the subject point up the fact that at least some of our difficulties result simply from force of habit.

My word, Mr. Speaker, do you mean to tell me that the government was obliged to have an extensive study made in order to show that the government has become a victim of habit? I would think it would be apparent to anyone who sits in this house or who reads the newspapers. But they had an extensive study made, and I guess it entailed extensive expense also. This pamphlet goes on to say this:
Spring to most of us is the traditional time to start clean-ups, remodelling, renovation and the general brightening up of our homes-
And it urges the people of this nation to try to place a few of these people who are out of work by doing their housecleaning early. Such drivel! Mr. Speaker, does the government not know that many of these home owners whom they are urging to do their spring cleaning early are the very ones who are out of work? They can do their own repairs around their houses if they have any money at all with which to buy lumber and paint. But I strongly suspect that many of these people will make no repairs to their houses this year because they cannot even afford the things they need in order to make the necessary repairs.
Let them get some whitewash from the government.

I am sure there will be plenty left over, judging by what we get in this house.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) spoke in Hamilton last Saturday and there were some press reports. Over the radio on Monday morning I heard this:
Labour minister Gregg has hinted at a large-scale housing program to take care of winter unemployment. The hint came in speeches to trade unionists and Liberal party members at separate meetings in Hamilton yesterday. He told the Liberals that federal authorities expect to be able to fight winter unemployment-especially in construction industries-with proper planning. To the trade unionists, he said that housing programs could have a sweeping effect on unemployment across the country.
In the Hamilton Spectator there is a report of the minister's speech in which we find the following:
The distinct possibility that construction work "almost throughout the winter" may become a reality in the not too distant future was envisaged on Saturday evening by the Hon. Milton F. Gregg, V.C., M.P., federal Minister of Labour-
Then it goes on to quote him as follows:
"We have discovered", said Mr. Gregg, "that with proper advance planning, there is no insurmountable reason why construction work should not continue throughout almost the entire winter each year, with the addition of only a slight extra cost to the work undertaken."

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Labour has made that discovery, why did he not put it into effect this year?
A very good question.

If there is to be a housing program which is going to have some effect on the unemployment picture, why was it not announced in this house? Why do these things have to be said to Liberal party organizations as, I presume, a chin-lifter at their regular meetings? This house is now in session. Why could it not be said here? Why does the minister not disclose to us what this housing program is, what these construction plans are?
It is not as well received here.

The government itself should take the lead and not call upon home owners to employ a few clean-up men in their back yards, somebody to shingle the roof or to paint the living room. The government has far more scope for employing people than all the householders of the country put together.
I should like to mention one matter which has been drawn to my attention and which I have mentioned before. It is one way in which the government could do something to level out the peaks and the valleys of employment in Canada. This one, as it happens, is related to my home town of Hamilton where we have the centre of the freight car industry in Canada. There we have the company which is the largest fabricator of freight cars in Canada. Also in Hamilton we have a company which produces castings and two companies which produce sheet steel. In Hamilton also is situated the company which produces air brakes. An informed guess as to the. number of workers who are engaged in the manufacture of freight cars and related production would be about 3,000 to 4,000.
At the present time freight car activity in Hamilton is at a standstill, and so far as I can ascertain there are no orders outstanding. In the past the requirements of the two railroads have averaged around 8,000 cars per year. In some years the orders have been less and in other years much more. I understand they have gone as high as 16,000 cars in one year. At the present time the placing of further orders has been deferred with the result that many workers now find themselves unemployed. Not once but many times, I understand, representations have been made both to the railways and to the government to adopt a policy of levelling out orders to avoid the very severe peaks and valleys in production which an ill-advised policy of purchasing has produced, a policy which has had an inevitable effect upon the
Unemployment
working conditions of so many people in my city. One of these railways is government controlled, and it is my opinion that the government should take the lead and set an example of properly controlled orders which would permit the supplying companies to revise their production schedules in order to provide year-round work for the employees in these plants.
There are other ways in which the government could assist in the present crisis, and not only in the present crisis but with an eye to a long-range program. I do not want it to be taken from my remarks that I think that public works in themselves are a cure-all for this situation. I do not. I think they play their part but I do not think that public works alone can cure the problem at the present time. However, I will say that we have one huge project in Canada which is away behind schedule. I refer to the trans-Canada highway in the completion of which alone there is plenty of work to be done. That highway was supposed to be finished in six years. Four of those years have gone by and only one-fifth of the road has been completed. There is apparent indifference on the part of the government to the situation of highways in this country. No one knows better than I that highways are a provincial responsibility, but the provinces have been kept plenty busy these past few years finding the funds to build highways within their own borders. There is still a crying need for through roads, roads to link provinces, roads to provide ready access to far places, roads which will provide the means of employment for the workers of tomorrow.
Despite the heavy taxes which flow into the federal coffers each year from the automotive industry alone, this country is far behind its neighbour to the south. We are not now back in the days of the horse and buggy when dirt roads were sufficient for local travel. The highway of today is as important as the railroads and the air lines, and it is about time that the government woke up to the fact that motor transportation is here to stay. In an article published in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, January 29, on this subject this paragraph appears:
If Ottawa continues to read the British North America Act but misread its Intent, there is a very real danger that the provinces, lacking a national blueprint, will spend millions of dollars and years of effort and time constructing the less important highways first.
I should like to point out the terrific importance of through roads in this country if for no other reason than that of military preparedness. The government has not hesitated to step into other departments of provincial authority and it is about time it

Unemployment
consulted with the provinces to determine the best way in which to pick up the slack in the construction of through roads which are so badly needed. Here is one more place where money could be invested wisely and well and, in the investment, provide employment for our people.
A nation, Mr. Speaker, is prosperous only as its people are prosperous. I think that is an accepted fact. A short time ago an editorial appeared in the Hamilton Spectator headed with the one word "If". It went on to point out the many "ifs" that have to be taken into consideration in looking at the Canadian economy. It asks what the government proposes to do about various things and then it says that probably things will work out well if-"if the economy of Canada today is not really, as it sometimes appears to be, a sort of Indian rope trick, up there in the sky with no visible means of support."
That "if" is what is bothering the people of Canada today right across the country. It is what prompts remarks by leaders of industry and leaders of labour unions alike, remarks of a nature we have not heard in Canada in many years. Wheat is unsold, markets have been lost, automobile inventories grow and grow so that one industrialist remarked only a very few days ago:
I'm very much afraid that we are in for more chaotic conditions in the auto industry in 1955 than we lived through in 1954.
He went on to say:
Don't ever forget this. We will never again experience the lush seven years we did during 1946-53. Those conditions are as dead as yesterday's newspaper.
The electrical manufacturing industry in this country has placed in the hands of every member of parliament a copy of the Knox report. Knowing full well that members of parliament are busy people they have also placed in the hands of every member of parliament a condensation of that report. The textile industry has been making representations to this government for over two years. Just this week a labour union presented its views on the condition into which the electrical manufacturing industry has fallen, recognizing that what affects that industry also affects its workers.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, history is being made when the members of a labour union take it upon themselves to present their views of the industry in which they are employed.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Trades and Labour Congress, the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Catholic confederation of labour, the association of mayors

and municipalities, the Canadian Manufacturers Association and other groups have spoken on this subject. They have all made their voices heard. There is no need to quote from their briefs; I am sure their contents are familiar to all the members of this house. I am certain that a good many hon. members have received telegrams from them today asking that their views be put forward in this debate. What are they worried about? They are worried about jobs, which mean purchasing power. They are worried about imports thrown on the Canadian market at prices below the cost of production here. They are worried about exports which they should be making to markets abroad. There has been a serious loss of markets for Canadian products abroad.
This is no time for complacency, Mr. Speaker. This is not a time at which we can say this situation will ease as the season advances. We cannot afford to wait. This is a time for action, and a time for both short and long-term planning. This is a time when we should take steps to provide jobs for our workers, a time when we should ensure that there will not be a recurrence of the situation in which we find ourselves today.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house, because of the grave state of unemployment in Canada as disclosed by the joint statement of the Department of Labour and the dominion bureau of statistics on February 23 last, the government should immediately give consideration to the formulation of plans to deal with this emergency, and to the necessary steps to establish a long-term program for expanding employment to be presented to parliament during the present session."

speakeroldname: Hon. Milion F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
I hope the leader of the C.C.F. party in this house will understand if I further delay the presentation of his case. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak in this debate immediately following the labour critic of the official opposition.
In some of the remarks my hon. friend has made from time to time she has indicated that perhaps the federal Minister of Labour lives in something akin to an ivory tower and does not get out in the country to learn what is really happening in the front line of labour activities. On Saturday morning I was engaged in discussions with labour leaders in her great city. I was rather hoping she would commend me for my visit to the city of Hamilton, but she did not see fit to mention it. I must say, however, that I came away from Hamilton on Saturday night greatly encouraged both from the point of view of the immediate market for steel and

from the point of view of the question which we are discussing at this particular time as it relates to Hamilton.
I am going to agree with my hon. friend from Hamilton West that the present unemployment situation does cause us great concern, but I am also going to say that this house should not conclude that we are confronted with a totally black picture. Far from it. I cannot even agree with the words my hon. friend used in describing the situation as a crisis in the history of Canada so far as unemployment is concerned. I do not believe that this is true. I do not frequently impose long speeches upon the members of this house, but in a little while I am going to present the over-all picture on employment as I see it. I shall try to do this without any "double talk" and without any appearance of "flippancy".
My hon. friend devoted a good deal of time to statistics. I agree that statistics are important, and a little later I am going to discuss statistics despite the fact that some people feel that we have too many statistics, particularly on this matter. At the outset and without any apology I am going to speak about the two sets of figures we issue every month, which cover the situation for every four weeks' period. Each of these two sets of statistics is designed for a special purpose and the two sets contain as much definite information as it is possible to obtain with regard to the employment situation in Canada without tremendous canvassing and census taking. Statistics compiled in the latter fashion would be out of date before they became useful for general purposes.
It is interesting to point out that the dominion bureau of statistics survey is generally in agreement with the statistics issued once every month by the department of commerce of the great country to the south. Statistics so compiled take the general form which was discussed and decided upon at the world statistical conference held at Geneva about a year ago. I do not wish to give the impression that because of this fact I believe the statistics are perfect. I think, however, it should be borne in mind that the statistics which come to us every month from the United States are comparable with the figures issued by our dominion bureau of statistics.
In listening to some of the statements made by my hon. friend one could easily get the impression that nothing is being done in relation to unemployment. I have already said that the unemployment situation this winter is a matter which causes us considerable concern. Most certainly we are concerned about those workers who have not been able to
Unemployment
secure aid through their unemployment insurance or through provincial or local arrangements. For this reason this government introduced an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act at the very outset of the session. I reiterate today what I said at that time, that the amendment deals with only one phase of the act, namely an improvement in the supplementary benefits. This in no sense meets the entire problem of unemployment which exists this winter. That problem will not be solved by waving a magic fairy wand over the country. It is not going to be improved by the introduction of controls in our economy at this stage, as was suggested by my hon. friend from Hamilton West.
I shall have to rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I did not mention controls at all. I referred to the levelling of orders.
I am sorry. I understood my hon. friend was suggesting that the federal government enter into the activities of those industries and exercise control.
She said no such thing.
Not at all.
She said no such thing.

If I misinterpreted her, then I regret it. These supplementary benefits have been in effect since January 10. In mentioning them now, I am not going to stress them, more than to say that they have been one factor this winter in alleviating the effects of unemployment in Canada. The remainder of the amendments to the act will be coming to the house this month.
There are however a number of other and, I would emphasize, equally positive steps that we in the Department of Labour have been taking in recent months. To those I shall refer later. But, Mr. Speaker, in looking at this matter in a calm and dispassionate way, as I am sure we must, I do not think we should overstate the case, nor do I think we should understate it. Certainly I am going to try not to do either today.
But if we take a look at the situation, as the amendment suggests, from the broad point of view, every member in the house will agree that the greatest ally in the maintenance of employment, and to bring about the fullest possible employment, is in the realm of good labour-management relations. In making that statement I am going to say immediately that, as everybody knows, the great majority of workers in this country come under the jurisdiction of the labour laws of the ten provinces of Canada. The provincial department of labour are doing a great job

Unemployment
in this field, and today I pay a tribute to them; because in their fields as well as in our own- but particularly in their fields-there have been very few recent labour disputes that have culminated in strikes. There have been two outstanding ones now settled. The first of these was the Ford strike, which was settled not so long ago-and we were all happy about it. This was followed by the Chrysler dispute settlement. While these disputes were within the automotive industry they also were important in their second, third and fourth repercussions on other industries which provide materials and supplies.
In her remarks my hon. friend mentioned the difficulties being experienced by our municipalities across the country. Although there is no way at all by which the federal government can or should act over the heads of the provinces and deal direct with the municipalities, nevertheless I, like her, am concerned with the situation in those municipalities. Perhaps we should not have done so, but from time to time members of this government have met and discussed unemployment problems with the representatives of many municipalities at their request, particularly within Ontario. Basically they have what is a serious problem in connection with what we have come to call the unemployables. I do not like the word very much, but it refers to those people who for the time being are not able to work to earn a livelihood. A very great deal has been done in recent years by all levels of government and by private agencies on behalf of those who are in this group, who are handicapped in their ability to work and to earn a livelihood. One can think of all kinds of examples on a national scale, as well as those on the provincial and municipal levels. There are such outstanding ones as the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Canadian Tuberculosis Society, and many more. Thank heaven we have them in Canada, on the national as well as the local scale.
In recent years these are backed up by such provincial agencies as the provincial workmen's compensation plans, then there is the federal-provincial rehabilitation plan, which takes in three or four departments of provincial governments, three departments of the federal government, the municipal governments and a whole array of private agencies at all three levels.
And there is now, this winter, the federal-provincial pension plan for those totally disabled civilian members of our population who cannot work at all. And, finally, there are arrangements existing in some parts of the country for local assistance of those people

who are left out of all these other agencies. They can be and are being given relief by local agencies or governments. Sometimes it is in co-operation with provincial governments, and sometimes it is not.
I believe that in this field I have just mentioned we in Canada as a country-with the provinces, the municipalities and the great agencies that are working in those fields- have made very great strides during the past four or five years; and in that we can take some joint satisfaction.
Now a word about the very much larger number of people today who are fit and able to work but who are without employment. They are the ones to whom my hon. friend has referred. The great majority of these workers are protected by unemployment insurance to tide them over until work can be found again, and to augment whatever they may have been able to save during their employment prior to losing their jobs.
But I have been very well aware of the fact that there are others who are able to work, but who are without jobs and are not receiving unemployment insurance benefits. In some cases local authorities on whom the responsibility for these workers falls are providing aid either alone or, in some instances, with the provinces. And while several municipalities in the province of Ontario- quite a number as a matter of fact-have made representations directly to the federal government on the problem, neither the government of this province of Ontario nor of any other province has stated that the problem had reached proportions beyond their capacity to cope with it.
The unemployment this year has added to the number of cases requiring assistance by local agencies, and particularly in industrial centres. As the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) knows-because he was present-we had a case in point last Friday.
Would the minister permit a question?
Yes.

The minister has disclaimed any intention of understating the problem. May I ask him if he would describe the extent of unemployment in Canada today- the first day of March-as it was described in the speech from the throne on January 7, when these words were used:
Some unemployment of a regional and seasonal nature is being experienced.

If my hon. friend will recall, in the early part of my remarks I promised that later on I would discuss that matter. At the moment I am discussing the situation

affecting welfare. I am more interested in what is happening to these people-whether they are suffering from hardships-than I am in quoting figures. But I shall put the figures in, just the same, a little later on.
Now, while there has been a recognition of growing need in this area I have been talking about, it has not led to any mutual understanding between federal and provincial governments as to the action that should be taken in the matter. This government has not been unconcerned about the problem. Notwithstanding the primary responsibility of the provinces in this field, the federal government is prepared to discuss with them the problems of this group of unemployed workers, as an item on the agenda of the forthcoming federal-provincial conference, if the provinces request that that be done. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that that will be the answer to the hon. member for Hamilton West who said that the problem she mentioned has been juggled around between governments. As far as this government is concerned, we do not want it juggled around any longer.

That was discussed by the
Prime Minister today in answer to a question, and I am sure he will reply to any question of my hon. friend's.
Next June will not help much now.

With respect to the remarks
made by the hon. member for Hamilton West, but not so specifically today as on other occasions, as to what the Department of Labour is doing about this and whether we were prepared to sit down, as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) said on one occasion, and allow these people to be abandoned and take no constructive measures with respect to them, I want to say that we in my department are active in this regard. I wish to pay a tribute today to the way in which Canada's workers, whether they are organized or unorganized, have met the strains and hardships that have been talked about in the discussion so far. The hardships have been greater for some groups than for others; but in nearly all cases there has been, on the part of those affected, a degree of mobility and adaptability that is highly commendable. I am referring here not only to the workers but also to those who manage the industries involved. I want to pause here and emphasize it. It is patently true-and the hon. member for Hamilton West may throw it back in my teeth-that in this country we must have
Unemployment
a greater mobility of working forces and a greater willingness and desire on the part of our working people to take advantage of the opportunities for employment that are coming up in North America's last frontier in the north. In spite of all the clashing of orders that has taken place, the way in which our workers have filled the needs in those fields is something of which we are very proud.
I will admit that some of the adjustments that we have made could have been less painful-I will put it that way-if we had continued, as some hon. members suggested, in all those years a tightly controlled economy such as we had in world war II. But I am convinced at the same time that this would have been at the price of progress in our country, and it would have lowered our standards of living and the working conditions of our workers.
I am sure there is no doubt in the minds of most Canadians that they prefer freedom and a change to tight control and a relative static state of affairs. I know that nobody in this house is advocating that, but I do think that sometimes when we say: let us do this, and let us do that; let us go into industry and tell them that they have to put this industry in this place, and then we are going to have a group of workers move over from point A to point B and work in that place, we forget that these things cannot be done without the kind of control that we had during the war, and we might as well face it.
When this government gradually lifted controls after the war, there were prophets of gloom who forecast that all sorts of consequences would come. There would be utter chaos and long and heavy periods of unemployment. Instead of that we have witnessed one of the most prosperous decades in our history. Despite the effects of the difficult situation that we already admit and which my hon. friend mentioned this afternoon, I believe that the confidence exhibited in the potentialities of our country, when the economic forces were given freedom to work, has completely justified all that. This freedom which has prevailed has been a factor in attracting to Canada the large investment which we have had during the post-war years. In spite of that old tough law of supply and demand that has worked and has left its results on some workers who could not get jobs, I am sure that if we had let that go as a tough law and had not provided anything at all to take up the slack and to protect them, we would have been very cruel indeed.
We could have said: it is too bad, but we must let it take its course. We would have

Unemployment
been callous if we had not injected something to help find jobs and alleviate hardship. As a matter of fact, some things have been done by very important agencies within my department. I am going to mention them again because they are working today in our country. In our over 200 employment offices across Canada we have well-skilled placement officers finding employment. In the calendar year of 1954 over 800,000 workers, in addition to those who found employment by other means, were employed through our offices. It may be interesting to know that in the month of January, 1955, in our offices across Canada 59,610 workers were found employment, which indicates that the 570,000 that my hon. friend mentioned a moment ago is not a static figure. It does not represent the same people from day to day, week to week or month to month. It is an ever-recurring figure of the number of workers who are often on short time unemployment.
This is a large operation, and I am grateful from time to time to find that those who are engaged in the task are doing things, as an American so well put it, over and above the ordinary call of duty.
Not so long ago the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. White), in his speech in this house, referred to the Belleville Ontario-Intelligencer. He said that the national employment service was acting as the rallying point for a drive on seeking winter jobs. The hon. member for Hamilton West did not think very much of this program. She accused me of announcing it in Hamilton instead of in this house, but I would remind her that on my estimates last year I went into this matter to some extent and made a report on it. I do not want to overemphasize it because it is not the whole cure for unemployment, but it is one of those things that can help. Furthermore, this winter was designed to be the first opportunity we would have to put a variety of experiments into effect.
Experiments such as are going on at the edge of Ottawa, at Mooretown, a subdivision being constructed under the supervision of the trades and labour council of Ottawa, which is being specifically worked out so that every item going into that undertaking shall be looked at from the point of view of the possibility of a greater amount of employment during the winter months, is'a case in point.
I should like to refer to the town of Pembroke. In Pembroke they took this matter under consideration at the suggestion of the employment committees and the local manager of the employment office as a job in hand. Without reading the full report, I will

say that all parts of the community are connected with it and the results have been very good. Representatives of management, representatives of unions, representatives of retail merchants, representatives of municipalities, of social organizations, of building and trades council, of the Petawawa military camp and of educational institutions, are on the committee. I could quote quite a number more, but I am not going to do that. However, the story would make interesting hearing.
The national employment committee is composed of senior representatives of the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Trades and Labour Congress, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the National Council of Women, the Canadian Legion, the Canadian Retail Federation and the Canadian Welfare Council. These ladies and gentlemen are most active in their own organizations and in the ordinary walks of life. They meet at regular intervals to consider this problem. They are joined at these meetings by members of the unemployment insurance commission, officials of my own department and any other officials of government who might be useful.
It is to that committee that thanks should go for encouraging this idea in the first place and for seeing that there was carried out a survey which made it possible to have a report which would act as a textbook for all those concerned that could do something about this. Perhaps I should refer for instance to the results as obtained in the city of Quebec, as well as in the city represented by my good friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and others, but perhaps that would take up too much of the time of the house.
However, I might refer to the fact that quite recently the Canadian Construction Association met with the government and pledged their full co-operation in this field in seeing that additional construction work was carried out during the winter months. There are those who may say, "Oh, well, you are going to do summer work in the wintertime". I point out the fact that this would not necessarily mean there would be less work during the summer.
Perhaps I could say just a word about industrial relations. Collective bargaining settlements of particular significance were reached recently in the automobile, radio, television broadcasting and shipbuilding industries. Most of the recent settlements affected provide for small wage increases and many are to be put into effect during the next two years. I have referred already

to the automobile settlement and the settlement in connection with the Chrysler Corporation of Canada. It is hoped that the settlement of these two disputes in the provincial jurisdiction will have an important impact upon the employment situation in the industrial area of southwestern Ontario which is so greatly affected at the present time.
I pass quickly over the dispute which was within the federal jurisdiction, and refer particularly to that affecting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) was very worried that he would turn on his radio and get no results.
The shipbuilding industry is in good shape at the present time. On the west coast there is a strike at the Burrard Dry Dock Company at North Vancouver, but this is the only strike there has been in that area for some little time.
As to public utilities, an agreement was reached between the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario and an independent employees association representing 10,000 office, operational and maintenance workers. The new agreement provides for a 4 per cent increase in salaries with certain other fringe benefits. The settlement of this dispute will have its good effect. In Saskatchewan contract negotiations are reported to be in progress between the Saskatchewan power corporation and the oil workers international union CIO-CCL representing approximately 1,200 workers of that crown corporation. The union's demand for a general wage increase, which appeared to be the main issue of dispute, was turned down by the board of conciliation.
I come now to textiles, which has been much in the public mind, certainly in the minds of the government during the past two years. I am not going into the causes for the decline in the textile industry this afternoon, but it is truthful to say that apparently the textile industry is not declining any more. Many will say, "Thank heavens, it has gone too far now".
Following a strike which lasted several weeks, an agreement was reached between two syndicates of the National Federation of Chemical Workers (CCCL) and the Dominion Oilcloth and Linoleum Company Limited, Montreal, and a subsidiary, Barry and Staines Linoleum (Canada) Limited, Farnham, Quebec.
In connection with chemical products, several collective agreements were bargained recently, mostly in Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland.

I should like to refer back to the matter of statistics. I do not want to minimize the seriousness of what we are discussing today. Fortunately as compared with earlier years in Canada we have a statistical record. It has been the traditional policy of the government, in fact of all governments, since the passage of the Employment Offices Coordination Act after world war I to publish employment service statistics. With the development of the unemployment insurance program and the expansion of the national employment service, statistical material reflecting the operations of the employment service has been extended. These operational figures are available and provide information as to the numbers of persons who use the employment service, their occupational and other characteristics, information which it is imperative to have.
That is a general statement and you may say, "What do you mean by that?". I said a little while ago that this problem is one which concerns us all. The things we can do can be most effective if they are attacked, as I mentioned about Pembroke, by a lot of people from many different points. We should be able to know how the situation is there or in any given city or town in Canada. As well as that, we should have the over-all picture. People who are moving or building or constructing in various parts of Canada should be able to know what the employment situation is in that area. I think a good example of that is this. Great contractors coming from all parts of the eastern half of Canada to the national defence construction at Camp Gagetown were glad to get through our employment service what manpower was available and where. For their purpose it did not matter very much whether they were exact, but they served as a good guide.
These operational figures cannot provide information on the over-all characteristics of

Unemployment
the working force and other adult members of the population. It was for this reason that the government some years ago decided to develop a comprehensive national sample survey of people of working age. This survey to determine the views of people across Canada with regard to their association with the labour force provides valuable data on the various broad categories of employed persons. It also provides useful estimates of the reasons people are not at work during that particular survey week. A similar national survey of the labour force has been made for a number of years in the United States. I will add what I said a little bit earlier, namely that this has been carried further now through the international labour office to other countries.
The national employment service data, on the other hand, provides us with a single figure of those who are registered for jobs. An effort is made to remove from this figure those people believed to be employed, but it is known that a considerable number of those registered at national employment offices at any one time will have found work other than through our local offices. From this single figure of applications for jobs we cannot tell much about the type of association these people have with the labour force, whether they are long-term or short-term, whether they have a job or are not working, and all that. As long as it is recognized that these registrations for employment at local offices, which I have said are operational statistics, and those estimated from the overall labour force survey as being without jobs and seeking work during the survey week, were never intended to measure exactly the same groups of people, there is no need for confusion at all, as I see it. I can inform the house that the people who are in fact utilizing these figures for practical purposes are not finding them confusing. I am convinced that we can tell much more about the over-all employment and unemployment situation locally and nationally through having both sets of figures than we should be able to do without them.

Will the minister permit a question? This is the question I asked before the orders of the day were called last Thursday. At that time the minister did not answer, and Mr. Speaker indicated he thought this was a question that might better be answered in this debate. My question was this. In view of the figures released by his department and the dominion bureau of statistics last Wednesday, do the minister and the government still consider unemployment today in the same terms in which they

described it in the speech from the throne, namely as seasonal and regional?
I am going to go right on now, if my hon. friend will permit me to do so, and then when I am through-
Shall I get my answer?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Does the minister refuse to answer?

If my hon. friend will wait until I have finished and then if he finds that I have not answered him, perhaps he would ask his question again. What I propose to do now, Mr. Speaker, is to give the house a summary of the unemployment situation as we see it across Canada at the present time. That perhaps will be the answer to my hon. friend's question.
At January 20 persons without jobs and seeking work were estimated in round figures-and my hon. friend referred to this-to number 362,000 by the D.B.S. survey, or 80,000 higher than last year. The number of persons registered at the national employment service was 570,000, again in round figures, 46,000 above last year. On the face of it, therefore, the unemployment situation may appear a good deal worse than last year, which might lead one to conclude that both the economic situation and the employment picture are deteriorating.
I stop there to refer to my hon. friend's reference to my Merry Christmas and Happy New Year message at the end of the year-

How about an Easter
message?

It is too soon. I also want to refer to the remark that it was double talk. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I have not often been guilty of double talk in this house. If my hon. friend thought I was guilty of double talk in my New Year's message, I can assure her that there was no such intention on my part. In discussing this question and trying to find the middle ground, the facts of the matter, it may be that sometimes it looks as though you are leaning a little further over to the right or a little further over to the left. But I can assure my hon. friend that our labour force in Canada is growing more rapidly than that of almost any other country in the western world, and we can easily have more unemployment and greater employment at the same time. She will admit that. Having admitted that, I shall return to my script. The employment picture-
And come to the question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Oh, yes.

I should like to point out that what I said was that we not only had more unemployment but that we had more people unemployed than the actual increase in the labour force itself; that the number of unemployed had increased.

I think I must disagree with my hon. friend there. I shall just go on from the point where I started.
At January 20 of this year persons without jobs and seeking work were estimated to be 362,000 under the dominion bureau of statistics survey, 80,000 higher than last year. That is the D.B.S. survey. The number of persons registered at the national employment service was 570,000 last month, or 46,000 above last year. I shall stop there. A while ago my hon. friend indicated that the labour force had increased by over 100,000. I should have the figure-
The labour force increased by 145,000 and those unemployed by 175,000 in the same period, a two-year period between January 1953 and January 1955.

I will proceed from there, Mr. Speaker. On the face of it, therefore, the employment situation may appear a good deal worse than last year, which might lead one to conclude that both the economic situation and the employment picture are deteriorating.
Hear, hear.

This is not the case. I say that with all due respect for my friend the hon. member for Eglinton. In fact the employment picture during the last six months is a good deal better than was the case last year.
This is triple talk; this is not just double talk.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

From September to January of last year the number of persons with jobs in non-farm industries declined by 211,000. This year the economy lost 50,000 fewer jobs than a year ago during this period of seasonally declining employment. Thus the underlying trend of industrial employment is stronger than it was last year. Because total employment in January this year was the same as last year, and it was, almost all of the increase in unemployment is due to the growth in the labour force. In January, 1955, the labour force was 72,000 higher than was the case last January. If we look at the increase in the
Unemployment
labour force since September last year compared with the year before we find that the great change contributing to unemployment was in the non-agricultural labour force. Last year over this period the non-agricultural labour force decreased by 21,000 whereas this year it increased by 32,000, or a net growth of 53,000 in the non-agricultural labour force. This, as can be appreciated, has been the major factor contributing to our higher year to year level of unemployment. The increase in unemployment has been no greater this year than last year considering the fact that we have been at higher year to year absolute levels.
The minister has been living in an ivory tower.

Perhaps my hon. friend will wait, as I sometimes do with his speeches, until the end of my speech. Between December and January of this year the percentage increase in unemployment was the same as last year although, of course, the absolute increase was greater. Between November and January the rate of increase this year was considerably smaller than last year, being 85 per cent last year and 70 per cent this year. I am not bragging about this; I am just stating facts.
May I ask the minister if he still says that the situation is not deteriorating as compared with last year?
The employment situation is not deteriorating compared with last year, no.
Then the minister must be living in an ivory tower.

This increase in unemployment has taken place at the same time as productivity has risen as a result of increased competitive pressures at home and abroad. This has, in fact, meant that some weaker firms have had to close down. Other firms have succeeded in increasing output without increasing employment and have tightened up on their use of manpower in their effort to overcome high labour costs. Again, I am trying to be factual. For example, while total industrial production during 1954 increased to approximately 4 per cent, employment remained stable throughout the year. Total output in manufacturing remained quite constant during 1954 while employment in manufacturing declined by about 5 per cent. These productivity gains have had a double barrelled effect. Rising productivity has strengthened the competitive position of the Canadian economy in export and domestic trade, thereby putting our industries in a stronger position to increase employment in the future. This year,

Unemployment
however, it has meant displacement of labour and has contributed to our unemployment problem.
While there has been little change in the level of total employment over the past year, there has been a considerable strengthening of employment in many industries. On a year to year basis, employment in the forestry industry is up. In the mining industry it is up 7 per cent, in public utilities 4J per cent, in trade 0-5 per cent, in finance, insurance and real estate 6 per cent and in the service industries 2 per cent. Employment in manufacturing industries has shown divergent trends. While it has declined in a number, it has risen in others. A further favourable development has been the increase in the number of hours worked in manufacturing. Throughout most of 1954 the number of hours each week averaged considerably less than in 1953. This gap narrowed rapidly towards the end of the year and at the beginning of December the number of hours worked was the same as in the previous year.
By themselves, of course, these increases in employment over the past year are not representative of the over-all situation. There have been a number of employment declines which have been more than seasonal in character. Perhaps that partly answers my hon. friend's question.
A very small part.

Such declines have been concentrated in manufacturing and these have tended to offset employment gains so that total employment has remained stable.
Although there are a large number of workers currently registered with the national employment service, the great majority of these are receiving or will shortly be receiving unemployment insurance benefits. At the end of January of this year there was a total of 543,300 people claiming regular unemployment insurance benefits. Not all of those who claim unemployment insurance benefits, of course, receive them. Some claims are disallowed because the people concerned are not unemployed or are not really available for work. Others are postponed for varying periods because such workers voluntarily left their last job or for other similar reasons. By far the majority of people who make claims, however, receive benefits.
At the end of January workers actually receiving regular and supplementary benefits totalled 450,400, of whom 62,400 were in receipt of supplementary benefits. The amount of money at present being paid to workers as unemployment insurance benefits is very great indeed. During January, 1955, it totalled $28,372,400, of which $2,222,600 was in the form of supplementary benefits. Both regular
rMr. Gregg.]
and supplementary benefit payments this January were substantially greater than in the same month last year when they amounted to $25,149,900 in total, of which $1,202,700 was supplementary benefits. Since last November total monthly payments of regular benefits have risen by about $12 million, slightly less than the rise which occurred over the same period last year. Supplementary benefit payments, on the other hand, were almost twice as large this January as last. The reason for the big increase in the supplementary benefit payments is, of course, the recent amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which were brought in last January.
Employment in the five regions-I am going to go over them very quickly-has shown diverse trends during 1954. As all hon. members know, unemployment insurance offices cover the Atlantic region which includes the four Atlantic provinces and a small slice of Quebec, the province of Quebec which covers part of northern Ontario, Ontario which goes as far west as the head of the lakes, the prairie region which extends from lake Superior to the Rockies, and the Pacific region on the Pacific coast. Over-all employment in the Atlantic region, which fell considerably below year-earlier levels by June, 1954, has gradually increased during the latter part of the year and equalled that of a year ago by January, 1955. Unemployment in the region in January of this year was about the same as that of a year ago although in terms of its labour force it was slightly higher than that for Canada as a whole.
Employment in the Quebec region also fell somewhat more than seasonally during the first half of the year and failed to reach last year's level by January, 1955. While employment in the forestry industry has been running above last year's levels during the fall months, the decline in textiles, clothing and iron and steel industries has offset other employment gains. Consequently, the unemployment level has been running slightly above year-ago levels and in terms of the labour force of the region is somewhat above the average for Canada as a whole.
Total employment in the Ontario region has shown only a moderate pick-up during the latter part of 1954. By January, 1955, the over-all employment level in the region approximated that of a year ago. In this region a decline in manufacturing employment has been partially offset by higher levels of employment in construction and forestry industries. In terms of the labour force of the region, unemployment in January,

1955, was somewhat higher than that of a year ago, although still lower than the average for Canada as a whole.
Over-all employment in the prairie region has maintained a slight margin over year-ago levels during most of 1954, and this was also true of January 1955. While farm employment has continued to drop in this region, nonfarm employment has been rising at a considerable rate. However, despite the increase in employment, unemployment in the region increased above year-ago levels, although it might be pointed out that unemployment in this region was remarkably low during the latter part of 1952 and early 1953. Unemployment in terms of the region's labour force was somewhat below the Canadian average in January 1955.
The employment level in the Pacific region. after being below the year-earlier level in June 1954, rose fairly rapidly during the latter half of the year and by January 1955 was moderately higher than that of January 1954. The major impetus to this rise in employment has come primarily from the forest industry, where employment at December 1, 1954 was 10 per cent higher than the year-earlier level. While unemployment in terms of the labour force of the region has continued above the Canadian average, it was the only region in which the unemployment level was no higher than it was last January.
