members took part, was conducted in a very amicable fashion. I am sure all hon. members taking part made a valuable contribution, and there was little or no acrimonious discussion throughout the two days of the debate.
The statement made at that time by the then secretary of state, the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickers-gill) was noteworthy because, speaking for the government on the measure a year ago, he called off the whips, at least so far as his party was concerned, and said it would be a matter for the judgment of each member in the house. As reported at page 5663 of Hansard he said:
It seems to me that in relation to the election laws we, as members elected to this chamber, and not as members of the government or of the opposition, settle what the law will be. And it would not embarrass me in the slightest to find that the hon. member for Rosthern or the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir), or the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris), or any other member in the house took a view of this question different from the one I take.
I hope that view will be voiced again during the current debate by a member of the government. I believe if this bill comes to a vote in which hon. members are allowed to vote in line with their views as to the merits of the proposal, there is every chance that the bill will pass. But even if the bill does not pass, there is certainly every chance that it will receive substantial support.
I believe the time is not far distant when the voting age in Canada will be substantially reduced. The trend is already very evident. Three provinces in Canada have reduced the voting age to considerably below 21 years. In 1945 Saskatchewan reduced the eligible age for voters from 21 to 18 years. Saskatchewan was the first province in Canada so to reduce the voting age, and it remains the only province that has followed that course. But the governments of Alberta and British Columbia have reduced to 19 years the eligible age for voters in provincial elections. It seems to me those three examples are an indication of the trend to reduce the eligible age of voters.
A suggestion was made by the President of the United States to congress last year that the eligible age of voters in that country be reduced to 18 years, and I believe a reduction in the eligible age is on the way. It is only a matter of time until we in Canada will bring about a substantial reduction in the age of voters.
Because I believe that is so, and because I believe it is a laudable objective, I have presented this bill in the hope that that objective may become an accomplished fact at an

early date. I believe it is wise for Canada to provide the widest possible base in the matter of the eligibility of voters. Over the years property qualifications have gradually been abolished in elections; they are completely abolished in the federal law and in the law of most-if not all-of the provinces. Perhaps a majority of the municipalities still require certain property qualifications; and in those municipalities where property qualifications have been partially removed the requirement usually prevails that to have a vote a person must rent quarters having a certain annual rental value.
I hope the day will come when property qualifications in all our municipalities will be completely removed, because the fact that a citizen of a municipality does not own property does not mean that such citizen is not making as valuable a contribution to the life and welfare of the municipality as is the property owner. The very fact that a person lives in a municipality, produces wealth and pays rent is as great a contribution as though that person held a good deal of property.
So over the years the base for voters has been widened. Today women have the franchise; we have universal suffrage in Canada, with the eligible voting age of 21 years. Only the group between the ages of 18 and 21 now remain to be given the franchise. I suggest they should be given it because, on the basis of any standard the government may wish to put forward, Canadians between the ages of 18 and 21 can qualify just as readily as citizens of any other group. As a matter of fact statistics show that perhaps the best educated group in our nation are our younger citizens between the ages of 18 and 21.
This is a good sign, because it means that over the years the educational standards of Canadian citizens have been improved. In 1911, according to the census of that date, the average 18 year old citizen in Canada had a grade VII education, whereas 30 years later, according to the 1941 census, the average 18 year old Canadian had the equivalent of a grade X standard of education. This is an average improvement in the 30-year period of three additional grades of education. The 1951 census shows that educational standards have improved so that the average schooling of a Canadian citizen had increased in the ten-year period by one-half year.
This is just a statistical indication of a situation of which each member in the house is aware, that as the years go by Canadian citizens are becoming better educated and better qualified to cast intelligent ballots at elections. They are better qualified to vote at the age of 18 years, I suggest, than were their fathers or their grandfathers at the age

of 21. That is progress, something to be proud of; and we should recognize that progress has been made by reducing the eligible voting age.
It does not follow that when the eligible age is reduced to 18 years everybody upon reaching that age would vote automatically in a federal election. What it means is that when a federal election is held every four or five years, all persons of the ages of 18, 19 and 20 would have the right to vote. At present the average Canadian citizen casts his or her first vote in a federal election at the age of 22 or 23. If I may make a personal reference, in my own case I happened to be 24 when I had my first opportunity to vote in a federal election.
How did you vote?

Had the age of eligibility for voting been reduced I would have had the opportunity to vote at the age of 19. With a reduction in the voting age, perhaps the average age at which young Canadians would cast their first vote would be reduced from 23 to 19 years. Surely that is not a very revolutionary suggestion for a change in the voting age. I have seen at first hand in my own province that young people 18, 19 and 20, realizing that they have the right to vote in a provincial election, do in fact accept and discharge that responsibility, if I may say so, at least as capably as the persons in other age groups.
Somebody says, "Look at the result". Well, I imagine if the ballot were not secret it would be found that the opinions of the people in the younger voting group, on balance, are not too much different from the opinions of other persons in different age groups. I think that comment is borne out by and large by the result.

I was going on to attempt to prove that I did not expect the result would be altered very much, because in the years that we have had a provincial election in Saskatchewan we have had a federal election shortly after, and while there have been slight changes, the trend has been usually about the same and the result usually has not been very different.
I would expect that in the normal course of events on balance the younger people would have some newer ideas and would be able to bring some new thinking to bear on the different issues. I believe the contribution that can be made to public life in Canada by allowing the 18, 19 and 20 year olds to vote in elections would be a healthy one. I was about to point out that young people in those age groups take their right to vote in Saskatchewan provincial elections very seriously. As a matter of fact they consider it a very important obligation, and, from my own observation, I believe they accept their responsibility at least equally well compared with any other age group of voters. The public meetings that I have had the opportunity to address, particularly in provincial elections, have convinced me that young people come out to hear the issues that are being discussed.
I was about to make reference to a comment made in the debate last year by the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I said that the standard of debate was high and that no member had criticized substantially the point of view of any other hon. member. However, I noticed one comment by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that I felt weakened the argument he otherwise might have had. He made the comment that to bring in a new group of voters would be expensive; it would cost a good deal of money. Apparently he was advancing that as an argument against reducing the voting age. I cannot believe that the government would advance such an argument as something one could seriously consider as a reason for voting against this measure. I am hopeful that in this discussion hon. members will endeavour to show that there is an argument for the bill, if they cannot be completely convinced. I am hopeful that a free vote will be held so that hon. members may follow their own conscience and their own beliefs without any reference to party discipline.
I also mentioned that I was travelling in fairly good company in asking that the voting age be lowered. President Eisenhower, in his message to congress last year, urged congress

to amend the United States constitution so the eligible age for voters could be reduced to 18. He said:
For years our citizens between the ages o!' 18 and 21 have, in time of peril, been summoned to fight for America. They should participate in the political process that produces this fateful summons. I urge congress to propose to the states a constitutional amendment permitting citizens to vote when they reach the age of 18.
It was suggested in the debate last year that the matter of reducing the voting age had been taken care of as far as members of the armed forces were concerned, and that any reference to a reduction in the voting age in order that such persons might have some say in the decision on government policy with reference to peace or war was invalid. I suggest that is not the case; that our citizens of 18, 19 and 20 should, as President Eisenhower suggested, be given the opportunity to participate in the political process that produces this fateful summons. We feel that as young Canadians have entered the armed forces they have discharged their responsibility with great merit. They have shown themselves capable of taking technical training in many instances and operating successfully, perhaps more successfully than any other age group, the intricate apparatus of war.
I suggest that there is no argument for refusing to lower the voting age. In the debate last year the hon. member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Jutras) made a very interesting speech. In the first part of his remarks he admitted, as reported at page 5534 of Hansard:
...the tendency in this country-and indeed in many others-is to lower the voting age from 21 to 18.
But he might have left with the Minister of Justice the idea that caused him to ask the question he did during the discussion. He said there did not seem to be any very keen desire on their part to exercise their responsibility at the present time, but he went on to say:
Taking the results of the last election, if they were to follow the example set by their elders, that would seem to be an indication that there is not a very keen desire on the part of any particular group to go to the polls on voting day. According to the results of the last election, even the older people did not go to the polls in the numbers that they should have.
Well, as I said, if that argument is carried to its logical conclusion we should be raising instead of considering a reduction in the eligible age of voters. I am sure the hon. member for Provencher would not want such action taken in this house, and I suggest to

him that the argument he has advanced is scarcely sound. He went on to say, in another part of his speech:
I do not think it would be logical to have students or young people voting in federal elections when they did not have the right to vote in provincial or municipal elections.
My comment upon that statement would be that the federal government should give a lead in reducing the eligible age of voters. As a matter of fact, if such a step were taken it would not be giving a lead to all the provinces, it would merely be following the step taken by three of the provinces. However, it would be giving a lead to the rest of the provinces and I expect also to the municipalities.
The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) made a most interesting contribution to the discussion last year. He referred a number of times to his great interest in scholarships for young people, and then he had this to say, as reported on page 5538 of Hansard of June 4, 1954:
A nice question arises when one has to decide at just what age a young person who is wholly maintained by his parents should receive the right to vote.
I suggest that whether or not a young person is being wholly maintained by his parents should have nothing to do with arriving at a decision as to the eligible age of voters. I imagine that the average young person in Canada who is being wholly maintained by his parents is being so maintained because he is continuing his education. He is spending those years to better prepare himself for citizenship in this country. The fact that a young person is still in school at 18, 19 or 20 years of age means that he is preparing himself to make a greater contribution to the welfare of the Canadian nation in years to come. If that young person is ready to so prepare himself to make that greater contribution, I suggest that is no reason why he should not be given the vote.
Members of this group are not the only ones who have supported a reduction in the eligible age of voters. I noticed that the provincial Liberal convention in Ontario a year ago supported a reduction in the eligible age of voters to 18 years. I suggest that the provincial Liberal convention in Ontario was providing real leadership to the government here, and that its suggestion was sound. For many years the C.C.F. has supported a reduction in the eligible age of voters. We welcome this resolution from the provincial Liberal convention in Ontario supporting our position.
I hope the government will act. I believe the eligible age of voters will in time be reduced, and I submit that the best time to do it is now.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to reduce the voting age from 21 to 18 years. I appreciate that a large number of those in this age group have sufficient education and experience to exercise their franchise in a rational and reasonable manner, but on the other hand I question whether a sufficient majority of them have reached political maturity. I feel that to pass this bill after a summary debate of this type would not be doing justice to it; therefore I shall oppose its passage at this time.
I feel that a measure of this sort requires a far more extensive study than can be given to it in a debate of this type. When we recall the responsibilities of this age group in other fields we find that over the centuries in our civil and criminal law this group has been treated differently from those who are over 21 years of age. Under our criminal law we find that those in the 14 to 21 year age group are held responsible for their actions, but it must be remembered that in criminal matters the problem is not too involved. Criminal law requires only that there shall be a knowledge of the difference between right and wrong. It is a fairly simple matter, as it is something which is ingrained in the child practically from the time he is born.
On the other hand our civil law both under British jurisprudence, which takes in all of Canada except the province of Quebec where the Napoleonic code prevails, and under the code in the province of Quebec, we find that those under 21 years of age are protected. Account is taken of the fact that no man nor woman under 21 years of age has sufficient maturity to assume complete responsibility for his or her acts. In civil law there are many problems of a complex nature which must be carefully weighed in order to arrive at a rational decision which will not do harm to the individual himself. As a result the attitude of the law has been that with a few exceptions no person under 21 can bind himself without the approval of the court or of his legal guardian.
I think a similar parallel extends into the political field. Politics is very complex. The public are being continually bombarded with statistics, propaganda and literature from all sources. We have in this house four political parties. It even takes a great deal of study and reasoning for a member of this house to weigh the different issues and arrive at conclusions which he feels are satisfactory. Therefore I say that far more study should be given to this matter than can be given in a debate of this type.
To illustrate what are the feelings of some of those in this younger group I should like

Canada Elections Act
to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press. This consisted of a contribution by the editor of the Manitoban, the journal of the University of Manitoba students' union. It is indicated that the opinions expressed do not necessarily represent the editorial views of the paper. I quote:
A recent address by President Eisenhower contains passages which if acted upon by American legislators will provide support for a new domestic issue in Canadian politics.
The reference is to a speech in which the president expressed favourable sentiments towards renewed suggestions that the voting age for American elections be lowered, from its present level of 21, to 18 years. Since the end of the second world war pressure for amendments to election acts has arisen in both Canada and the United States. Proponents of the change most frequently advance the argument that, "if a man at the age of 18 years is old enough to fight, he is old enough to vote."
But such an argument is based more upon the sentimentality of reward, than upon reason. The criteria of being able-bodied, and of being capable of obeying commands (which are the primary requirements for the bulk of any fighting force) do not in themselves ensure that youths at the age of 18 are equipped to mark a reasoned and responsible ballot. The execution of a military command and the exercise of one's franchise are subjects of widely differing mental processes. Development of the latter remains a more formidable problem.
British law has traditionally recognized that "infants" between the ages of 14 and 21 years are responsible for their criminal acts, since they are presumed to be capable of differentiating between good and evil. But legal commentators maintain that this simple ability does not serve to indicate the existence of a similar capacity for reaching wise mental conclusions. No one will suggest that a child has perfected his mature development at the moment he attains the age of 21; but the grounds for a valid presumption, based upon the experiences of making a living, are greater than at the school age of 18.
To date, measures for reducing the voting age have been supported by minor political parties and protest groups on the Canadian scene. In order to curtail any broadened application of the "fighting age-voting age" philosophy, the government has extended ballot privileges to those under 21 who enlist for active military service. On the provincial level, only the C.C.F. government of Premier Douglas has undertaken to extend the franchise in Saskatchewan elections. Whether the political maturity of that province has been enhanced remains for conjecture.
Amidst increased discussion of electoral reform, it is significant that pressure for lowering the voting age has come less from youth groups, which would be properly affected, than from parties in search of political issues. Before Canadian parliamentarians consider amendments to the elections act, it would be well to remember that for most youths of 18, this is still a world of hot dogs, and popcorn, and the corner "jukebox". Only the sobering influence of a few years spent making a living will best produce that interest which is sufficient to ensure mature political thought. The process requires time, and in this at least, youth abounds.
That may be an oversimplification of the problem, but I think it presents some of the views of the younger group.

When we refer to the records of this house we find that on February 25 a motion was made and agreed to, which instructed the standing committee on privileges and elections, among other things, to suggest to the house such amendments as the committee may deem advisable. That is a fairly wide directive to the committee, and I think it would take in, in this particular case, the problem which is immediately before the house. I think this committee could give this problem far greater and far better study than could be given to it in the house. It could obtain the necessary information and the necessary opinions upon which to base its findings. If this information is made available to the members of the house, following the hearings held by the committee, I think it will assist members also in making a rational decision in this connection.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that in my opinion this bill should not be passed by this house at the present time but rather that the committee which has power to study this problem should give it consideration.

have listened with great interest to the remarks made by the sponsor of this bill. I thought those remarks were similar to those he made last year, when he introduced a similar bill. I have read with interest the speeches that were made last year during that debate, to some of which reference was made by the hon. gentleman.
In so far as my predecessor is concerned I would say this. I do not believe the main reason for the then secretary of state opposing the measure was based on the ground mentioned by the hon. member, namely that there would be an addition to the expense of government if the lowering of age was approved. I think his main reason for opposing it at the time was the fact that he thought, along with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), that the age of majority-which in this country is 21 years-should first be lowered before a measure similar to that with which we are concerned today should be considered. I think that was the main reason for his opposition, and I think my hon. friend will agree with me when I say that.
I do not propose to speak for long, but I should like to make a few remarks concerning the matter. I believe we are all in agreement that we should extend the right of franchise to as many Canadians as possible if we wish to discharge our duties to the people under our system of government. I think that attitude has been taken previously by members of the government. When reading previous debates concerning amendments

to the Canada Elections Act, some time ago I read certain remarks that were made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I just wish to quote a sentence from those remarks, which may be found at page 2171 of Hansard of 1951. On the introduction of a resolution similar to the one I myself introduced to refer the amendments to the Canada Elections Act to a committee, the Prime Minister said:
I think we are all agreed that it is desirable that under the act the franchise shall be exercised as widely as possible, and no one would wish to insist upon any rule that unduly diminished the possibility of any elector exercising his franchise.
I quote those words because I believe that is the guiding principle we all have in mind, namely that we should try to extend that right of franchise as much as circumstances will allow. But as I mentioned last Friday when moving to refer the Canada Elections Act to the standing committee on privileges and elections, there are obstacles in the way. There are serious objections to extending a privilege as important as this to certain classes of people. I do not think I would wish to object strenuously or with much vigour to this measure which is introduced by the hon. gentleman. However, I think there are reasons which would justify my attitude in opposing the measure because I feel that the time has not really come for this action to be taken.
The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Weselak), who has just taken his seat, has suggested that this matter could very well be studied by the committee on privileges and elections. I do not see any reason why this matter could not be brought up for consideration at some time during the sittings of that committee, but in my opinion there is no justification for referring it to the committee.
As I said before, I believe there are reasons which would justify people in thinking that this measure proposed by the hon. gentleman is premature. I think the first remark I would make on that score is that this is an extremely important matter, and we ought to be careful before we extend the right of franchise to a new class of people.
The sponsor of this bill has pointed out that my predecessor last year mentioned the question of expense. It is, of course, true that this consideration should not be a reason for opposing the measure. On the other hand, it is a known fact that to set up an electoral district is a costly matter. We also all know that elections cost the Canadian people a great deal of money. The matter of extending the franchise to another class of people, thus increasing the expense in connection with elections, is one which must be seriously considered.

The hon. member mentioned some provinces in Canada which have extended that right of franchise and which have lowered the voting age. He has mentioned the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. I think it would be an excellent idea to wait until the other provinces follow suit so we may have a better understanding of the attitude of the whole nation to the question of extending the franchise to this class. We would be in a better position to see what the results would be throughout Canada. However, I do not want to put this forward as a reason for opposing the measure. I do not want to say that we should necessarily wait for the other provinces to take the initiative, but it would afford us an opportunity to find out what all the people of Canada think about it.
Another reason I think the time has not yet arrived is the fact that I believe we should be concerned first of all with trying to extend the right of franchise to Canadians already on the eligible list but who are not in a position to vote. In other words I believe that first things must come first, and that we should try to extend the right of franchise to people who, because of certain obstacles or circumstances, are not in a position to exercise that right. We should deal with that matter first and so arrange things that as many Canadians as possible who come within the section of the act defining the voting age and the conditions of voting will be able to exercise the right of franchise. I refer to those over 21 years of age who are eligible to vote but do not do so because of circumstances that may arise.
Canadians who are abroad are prevented from voting under conditions that now exist, and I believe one of the important and serious studies the committee should make is to see whether or not the right of franchise cannot be extended to these people. Before we extend that right to another class of people,

let us see to it that those who are already qualified to vote under the act are able to do so, that the obstacles in their way are overcome so they can exercise their right to vote.
One of the main reasons mentioned last year by those who opposed this measure was the age of majority. I think we can safely say that in most countries of the world the age of majority is either 21 or over 21. It would appear that the argument advanced last year by my predecessor deserves consideration. He said that he thought the age of majority should be studied first before the age of voting is lowered.
The hon. member said that because of the education given our young people today and their greater maturity they are in a better position to exercise the right to vote than those who preceded them. That may be true, but I think quite a number of people will agree with me when I say that before the right of franchise is offered to those between 18 and 21 years of age they should be given a chance to gain practical as well as theoretical experience. In their studies they are accustomed to dealing with the theory of things, but I think the matter of giving them a chance to see what practice teaches should be given consideration before they are given the right to vote. The three years between the ages of 18 and 21 is the period in the life of a young man when he has his first contact with public affairs. I believe it is sound to think that these three years are very important to the young man so that he may learn about conditions in his own locality, his own province and the country at large. Such knowledge will influence his judgment, and will help him in making a choice as to those men he would like to see in public life, and the man he would like to represent him in the parliament of this country.

Mr. Speaker, had this been a resolution I probably would not have risen at this point, but since it is a bill and can come before the house again, and since the hon. member who moved the bill is not particularly desirous that it should come to a vote tonight I might say a very brief word or two about it. The hon. member for Assiniboia has covered almost all the grounds, so there is little I can do except associate myself with him in the desire that the bill be ultimately passed.

The hon. member for Assiniboia told us that on account of the electoral laws, which will not permit those under the age of 21 to vote, he was unable to cast his first vote until he was the age of 24. Since that was the age at which he entered the House of Commons I presume that my hon. friend had the good wisdom to vote for himself on that occasion. Perhaps I may suggest playfully that the government would not have welcomed his coming to the house at an earlier age.
I think we are all agreed there is no doubt that young people reach the age of maturity much earlier now than they did at the time when older people like myself were at the age of 18. I want to say a word or two about the people who have voted in provincial elections in Saskatchewan at the age of 18. I have found considerable enthusiasm and interest among a fair percentage of the young people who are just past high school age. I may tell the government that the boys and girls who were allowed to vote in the provincial election of 1952 at the age of 18 or 19 were very angry indeed that they were denied the right to vote in the last federal election. They blamed the government when possibly they should not have done so. I do not know, but at any rate they blamed the circumstances which denied them the vote in the federal election. Having become interested in the provincial election in 1952 they did not see, and it was difficult to explain to them, why they could not vote in the federal election of 1953.
It has been said here that young people show a lack of interest in political affairs and do not know quite what it is all about. In that respect they are not much different from some of their elders. I dare to make that statement because of the fact that usually only a small proportion of the voters of the country exercise their franchise. It is not very long, of course, since the same thing was said about women's suffrage that is being said about these students. It was said that woman's place was in the home, that she should not concern herself with political matters and so forth. History reveals that it was a long time before women were given the opportunity to vote. The suffragettes sought for it by devious means, including the smashing of windows. We will not go into that now. Women finally got themselves the vote, and we have universal suffrage in Canada.
I would like to touch upon a point which I feel has not yet been mentioned, and that is the matter of intelligence. From my experience as a school teacher I have some

slight knowledge of psychology. Psychologists teach us that intelligence does not continue to develop in the individual after he has reached the age of 18. In fact, most people reach the acme of their intelligence at 15 or 16 years of age. After that, intelligence does not increase. We would hope, however, that wisdom does.
Another point which has not been mentioned is this:	Political clubs and student
parliaments in both colleges and high schools are becoming more prevalent across the country. 1 take this to be a sign that young people are becoming more interested in public affairs than was the case some few years ago. I also maintain that you learn to do by doing. You learn to have an interest in political affairs by having an interest in political affairs. I suggest that process could be commenced at the age of 18 as easily as at the age of 21. After all, many of our older people are not considered to be very mature after years of experience with the general field of politics. I do not think it is right for us to tell our young people that they must wait until they are 21 before they can begin to develop an interest in public affairs. I suggest it takes from 2 to 10 years after the age of 21 has been reached before most people become politically mature.
Life being limited, I suggest that we should interest people in public affairs at an earlier age. Our boys and girls are being taught civics and citizenship in our schools, and many take part in public speaking clubs, political clubs and student parliaments. I feel that this interest could be maintained if they were permitted to vote at the age when their thinking has been trained on public affairs. When our young people are 18 we think nothing of sending them out to work______
Or off to war.

Yes, we send them off to war or out to work or we send them back to the farms and tell them to forget about politics and public affairs until they are 21. By some magical process we expect them to be endowed with wisdom when they reach the age of 21. I suggest that the interest in public affairs which is created in our high schools and colleges should be continued, and that the next logical step is to turn the eyes of our young people to the field of public affairs and the politics by which such public affairs are governed. Some of our young people, of course, will take no more interest in politics than their parents did. They will probably vote as a matter of routine, and will follow the political opinions held by their parents. It is all right to follow the political persuasion of their parents, but I suggest that 50433-103^

The Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard) in objecting to this amendment said it was premature. I have no doubt that this was said about women's suffrage. I fancy that even the Secretary of State would not be so bold as to suggest that the giving of the vote to women was premature. The only argument which was presented in which I could see any logic whatever was that this amendment might require further study. I do not know, nor did he say, how he is going to conduct that further study.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He might discuss it with his children at home.
It is not my desire to plunge my hon. friend into difficulty.

It is six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mrs. Fair-clough.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we listened to two speeches, one by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough), who made some well-deserved criticisms of the government's policy and of the situation as it exists today, and the second by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg).
The minister began by telling us that the present unemployment situation causes concern. But it seemed to me that as he proceeded with his address, which I found rather difficult to follow, he ended by trying to tell the house and country that the increase in the

Unemployment
unemployment figures in the country at this time is due very largely to an increase in the labour force.
Now, if we look at the figures we find that we have more unemployed than we had four years ago; but we have also more people available for work. And if we compare the various percentages of unemployment with the total number of workers available we find that the picture is entirely different from the one presented to us this afternoon by the Minister of Labour. The 296,000 unplaced applicants in March 1951 were 7'8 per cent, or nearly 8 per cent of the total number of workers available for work-that is, the paid workers plus those who were seeking work.
At the present time I believe we are approaching a figure of some 600,000 persons who are seeking work in Canada, and this works out at some 14J- or 15 per cent of the labour force. Or, if we take the other set of figures, the 170,000 persons without jobs and seeking work in 1951, we find that was 4J per cent of the workers available for work. If today there are 362,000 without jobs, as we are told there are, then that is something over 8 per cent of the labour force. So the persons without jobs and seeking work are proportionately very much greater in number than they have been in preceding years.
We were told, too, by the Minister of Labour this afternoon that there had been a general increase in production during this period. That, of course, is true because of the increased efficiency of industry and because of new industrial machines. No doubt if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) were to speak in this debate he would tell us that the gross national product has increased over those years. That also is true, and his estimate is that it will increase further in the coming year. But it seems to me that if that is good for the country, as it should be, then we should have a diminution rather than an increase in the number of unemployed this year over preceding years.
The amendment states, of course, that the government should immediately give consideration to the formulation of plans to deal with this emergency, and to the necessary steps to establish a long-term program for expanding employment. I am thoroughly in accord with that, but what does the official opposition mean by those words? I know what we would mean if we had used them in an amendment we moved, and indeed in the amendment I might have moved this afternoon we had a phrase somewhat similar to the phrase I find in the amendment offered by the official opposition. If we are going to plan, and take the necessary steps to establish

a planned long-term program for expanding employment, then I believe we have to do many things that hitherto we have not done. And that, of course, is what we believe should be done.
The Minister of Labour this afternoon spoke about the necessity of people who were unemployed finding opportunities elsewhere, and he mentioned once again the necessity of the mobility of labour. But as a matter of fact what we have been doing over the years in relation to housing, for example, is to make less mobile our labour force. We in this party have urged the government again and again to establish rental housing projects in order that those who wish to seek work elsewhere than where they are located may rent homes, and not be tied down by homes they have had to purchase in the districts in which they live. It seems to me there is a conflict in ideas when the Minister of Labour suggests that there should be greater mobility in labour and that persons should seek work opportunities in districts other than those in which they live, if we tie them down in various localities because we refuse to adopt a housing scheme based on low or moderate rentals.
This afternoon we heard a great deal about the figures wholly related to the unemployment problem, but tonight I wish to deal with the subject from a slightly different angle; because I believe a significant feature of our unplanned economic system in North America is that between wars unemployment, and something which always accompanies unemployment in this country, namely falling farm prices, invariably plague the producers of wealth, whether they are industrial workers or workers on the land. We in this party believe that a country with abundant resources, such as the one in which we live, a country with fertile land and an intelligent and virile population, together with modern machinery, should be able to provide for full employment and proper returns to the farmer. And of course this also means a high standard of living for all the people in this country.
In wartime we had full employment, accompanied by relatively good returns to agriculture. This brought a widespread improvement in the standard of living of all the people of Canada, particularly those engaged in industry and agriculture. The fact that this does not happen in peacetime indicates, we think, a basic weakness in our economic system, a weakness which movements like ours were founded in all the democratic countries to bring before the public for ultimate solution.
It is I think significant that falling farm returns during the past several years have

been accompanied by rising unemployment. If one draws a graph showing farm returns and watches the fall and then the rise in a similar graph relating to unemployment, he will see immediately the connection between the two. In my mind the two are inseparably linked, as they were of course in the years of the pre-war depression.
Net farm income has fallen substantially in these post-war years. The dominion bureau of statistics-and I quote their figures because they are a government agency- shows that, in round figures, net farm income in 1951 amounted to $2,155 million. In 1952 it was $1,901 million; in 1953 it was $1,657 million, and the unofficial estimate for 1954 which, from what I have learned, I believe is going to be very close to the official estimate, is $1,200 million. There you have a striking fall in farm returns, accompanied at the same time by alarming, rising unemployment in our cities.
Let us look at the unemployment, and then we shall see how closely they are related to the farm figures and follow the same sort of pattern. On January 25, 1951, as reported by the dominion bureau of statistics, the unplaced applicants for work numbered-I want to use round figures again, and this was a labour department report-294,000. A year later, on January 24, 1952, the labour department release gave the figure as 350,000. On January 22, 1953, the figure had risen to 384,000. On January 21, 1954, it had risen to 523,000, and on January 20 of this year, the last return which we have available to us, the figure was 569,000.
These are unplaced applicants for work. But some of these of course the government will contend, and did contend this afternoon, were employed already and seeking new jobs. If we look at the other release, the labour department release of persons actually without jobs and seeking work, we find that in January, 1953, there were 187,000 without jobs and seeking work, in January, 1954, there were 280,000; and in January, 1955-and this again is the official labour department release-the figure was 362,000. I am not quarrelling about which set of figures we should use, because I think they both indicate the same sort of disease, but whether we take the figures of the unplaced applicants for work in the years under consideration, or whether we take those actually without jobs and seeking work, the increase each year since 1953 has, in my opinion, been nothing short of alarming.
All the minister could tell us this afternoon was that the present situation was causing the government concern. We had been told in each of those years that there was
Unemployment
nothing to worry about. We had contended that there was a great deal to worry about, but we were simply not listened to.
In January, 1955, there were almost twice as many people without work and seeking it as there were in January, 1953. In other words the number had increased from 187,000 to 362,000; and remember, I am taking the number without work who were seeking jobs. I am not, therefore, as I have said, going to take any exception to the difference between the two sets of figures. Both sets of figures indicate the tragic situation in which many thousands of Canadians and their families find themselves at the present time.
I said last year, after very careful examination of the trends in unemployment since the war and the equally significant fall in farm prices, that this winter would witness the worst unemployment situation we had faced not only since the end of the war but since 1940. I said at the time that all Canadians might not feel directly the effect of this serious situation, but that all of us would in time be indirectly affected to some degree by the misfortunes of so many of our fellow citizens. Apparently the government did not believe the situation would be as serious as it was last year, and it has done nothing effective to mitigate, let alone remedy, the problem. There has been no public works program or anything of the kind that would give relief to those who are unemployed.
It may be argued that the government, as the minister indicated this afternoon, had increased unemployment benefits by making some supplementary payments. But supplementary payments and unemployment insurance are not a cure for unemployment, they are merely palliatives. The only cure for unemployment is the provision of work, the finding of jobs.
In their presentations to the government last autumn the trade unions warned also that unemployment would be higher this winter than the previous year. In reply the Prime Minister, it will be recalled, said he felt that those pessimistic predictions would not be realized, and this winter unemployment would not reach last winter's postwar high. The official figures I have quoted sadly belie the judgment of the Prime Minister and the government. Unemployment now stands at a post-war peak. There is no doubt about that. All official figures very clearly indicate it.
I believe there is ample justification for the contention which I and my colleagues in this group have made on very many occasions, that unemployment in Canada is intimately related to falling farm income. Those

Unemployment
parallel trends I contend, Mr. Speaker, are not accidental. The decline in farm income is intimately reflected in the decline of farm purchases of manufactured goods of all kinds, and more particularly in the purchase of farm machinery and farm equipment and supplies. The result is that in the cities where farm implements and farm equipment have been manufactured there has been an acute unemployment situation since last summer. It is not surprising, then, to find that the workers in the farm implement industry, for example, are suffering acutely. They have gone to the trouble of preparing a brief in which they support-and I think this is significant-not meeting the unemployment particularly by the provision of public works and so on, but the fact that they believe it is necessary to maintain a prosperous agriculture because they recognize that they cannot be fully employed unless agriculture is prosperous.
Then you have the lay-offs of railway workers. They are not altogether due to the same cause. To some extent in some of the towns, as I have reason to know in my own constituency, the lay-offs have come about on account of the dieselization of the railways; but in the main the lay-offs on the railways are related to the. depressed condition of the agricultural industry. In many other ways the decline of something like 40 per cent in farm income in the last three years is having an effect on the general prosperity throughout the whole of this country.
It is paradoxical that in this land of plenty there should be people who, because of unemployment, have to reduce their purchases of protective foods. That was the case in the 1930's under the government then in power; or should I use the plural, because while we think of the Bennett regime, that was succeeded by the regime of the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, and during the whole of that period it was the case. In a land of plenty there was inadequate relief and virtual starvation. And it is the case today though to a less extent among some of the families in Canada. They are unable to buy the protective foods that the farmers produce. We find a condition of falling farm prices accompanied, as I have said, by unemployment in the cities.
The question I am going to ask is this. What is the government going to do about all this? That is the question which this debate raises very sharply today. So far this afternoon the Minister of Labour has indicated no solution for the problem. It seems to me that so far Canada has been following a policy of too little, certainly too late, when we consider that this is the month of March and winter is passing.
[Mr. Coldwell.l
Last year we were told that the unemployment figures were too small to warrant premature action on our part. We are told again that much of Canada's unemployment is seasonal or due to improved technology; that these types of unemployment are unavoidable and that they must be accompanied not by a recession, of course, but on the contrary by progress and prosperity.
I think such an attitude is fundamentally wrong and will lead us into more serious difficulties as the days pass. This afternoon we were told that in the last ten years Canadians have been more prosperous than ever in their history, that there has been more employment and better farm prices. I am not going to dispute that, but I am going to say that that was not anticipated when the war ended. Only the action of the United Nations in setting up UNRRA, the Marshall plan, the threat of war and the rearmament programs were responsible for those ten years of prosperity of which the government boasts today. Nothing the government has done brought that about; it was brought about by factors beyond the control of the government except in so far as we contributed to UNRRA and to the Marshall plan, and engaged in rearmament.
As I have said already, in a country like Canada with our resources and machines there should be more jobs to fill than there are men and women to fill them. If we look across the ocean we see a situation in Great Britain where full employment exists with far less resources and with the need to recover from devastation after the war. That picture in contrast to ours should fill us with shame.
It seems to me that the major responsibility of the government is to see that the pace of economic progress is not allowed to slacken until all the needs of the country are filled. Today plants are idle, men and women are unemployed and the standards of living, not only of those directly concerned but of all Canadians, are threatened by this condition.
There was a different attitude on the part of the government in 1945 when there was widespread gratitude by the government and of course by the people of Canada for the efforts made by our farmers and industrial workers during the war years. It appeared then that the government recognized its responsibility and announced that it was drafting a program for continuing full employment for Canada. At the dominion-provincial conference of 1945 the present government actually made specific proposals, which most of us, including myself, felt if put into effect would help to maintain full employment in Canada. The federal government proposed

certain measures including public works projects that would help to alleviate the hardships of those who in spite of plans to maintain full employment happened to be temporarily unemployed.
Those proposals were aimed too at taking the responsibility off the shoulders of the provincial governments. This afternoon we heard the Minister of Labour say that the primary responsibility for the care of and assistance to the unemployed lies in the provincial governments and the provincial legislatures. That is a different attitude from that taken back in 1945 by the present government at the dominion-provincial conference. Let me quote part of the statement that was made at that time:
As a part of the general arrangement with the provincial governments the dominion government now proposes to establish a practicable and comprehensive system of assistance to able-bodied unemployed persons as soon as possible rather than waiting until the need for it actually arises. It is thought necessary not to permit the recurrence of the problems of administration being separated from financial responsibility, and to avoid the makeshift arrangements and controversy with provincial governments which otherwise would be almost certain to recur under the old methods of providing relief even though the number of persons involved were small.
The government then proposed, as they said, to do something before the need arose; not, as we are discussing now, after the need had become evident and the situation had become alarming. Nothing was done and now they refuse, ten years later, to institute an emergency program to meet the situation even when the need has become both urgent and apparent at the present time.
We have heard members of the government pleading that its responsibility does not extend to these matters. We heard it this afternoon. Indeed, the federal government has pushed the responsibility for caring for the unemployed back to the provinces and the municipalities when the fall in farm returns, which I regard as a principal reason underlying the present situation, is the result not of provincial policies but of federal policies. In a recent brief of the Ontario welfare council, they make this telling point when they say:
It was clear that those who attended our meeting did not accept general statements that this problem represents no responsibility of the federal government. Since employment and unemployment are a national concern, it is self-evident that the fate of unemployed employables is similarly basically sensitive to federal initiative.
It seems to me that is what the federal government also said ten years ago, in 1945, at the end of the war. We of the C.C.F. have constantly urged upon the federal government that it should assume, as it indicated in
Unemployment
1945, full responsibility for all able-bodied unemployed. Not only did the government in effect admit this responsibility at the dominion-provincial conference but-I am going to emphasize this-when we signed the United Nations charter nearly ten years ago Canada undertook the threefold pledge of planning to achieve, and I quote the exact words of the charter-
-higher standards of living, full employment, and conditions of economic and social progress and development.
Let me add too that such a policy is the only effective answer to propaganda either of the communist or fascist variety. Let me say that when you have a situation like we have at the present time, which may become worse as the days go by, you will find that these incipient dangers do exist in a country where the standards of living fall and unemployment rises. These are the seedbeds. Hitler rose to power because of unemployment in Germany, and communist parties have risen to strength and power because of unemployment and distress. When we talk about containing communism we should begin in our own country by bringing about conditions such that incipient fascism and communism cannot arise.
Five years ago the secretary general of the United Nations appointed a group of experts on the problem of full employment. Their report, which was submitted in December, 1949, made three main recommendations. I want to put them on the record because they are in line with the philosophy and policy which the C.C.F. has preached throughout the years in this country. Summarized they are: First, that each government should adopt and announce a full employment target which will define the meaning of full employment in the country concerned.
Second, that it should announce a comprehensive program for directing its fiscal and monetary policies, its investment and production planning, and its wage and price policies, including anti-monopoly policies, to the continuous achievement of its full-employment objective.
Third, a whole series of policies that would help to expand effective demand, such as increased social security payments, lowering of the.incidence of taxation of the low-income groups, raising the standards of expenditure for education and health, and by means of other support to personal consumption, and by maintaining adequate and stable prices for agriculture.
The group went on further to advocate the control of monopoly prices to serve the interest of increasing consumer demand through the reduction of profit margins.

Unemployment
That is precisely the kind of program we have been preaching in this house and in the country. We have been urging Canada to maintain the high level of employment which we call "full employment". I know there are times when there must be some unemployment, but never the unemployment of 8 per cent, 5 per cent or 15 per cent, as unemployment has risen from time to time in the past. We have been urging Canada to maintain the high level of employment which we call "full employment", adequate returns for our farmers and a measure of prosperity for all our people. We believe these things are linked together, that they cannot be separated, and are possible.
Although Canada is a member of the United Nations and is aware of these recommendations, it has refused to take the initial steps to carry out either the charter, the pledges of the dominion-provincial conference or the recommendations of experts appointed by the secretary general of the United Nations. There has been much vague talk about maintaining a high level of employment which, I say, means substantially "full employment" but which, it seems to me, may mean anything or nothing to our present government.
I recollect that in 1950 my colleague the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) put on the order paper a question inquiring whether the government had done as the United Nations report suggested and had set up a full employment target. Viewed in the light of present conditions the government's answer is interesting, for it said this in part:
A rigid target in terms of a single objective-
And full employment was the objective under consideration.
-is generally considered oversimplified and unrealistic, particularly for an economy like that of Canada.
In other words, the government said that the aim of full employment set forth in the United Nations charter which we signed was unrealistic. During the war, however, we directed all our energies to a single objective. That single objective was the winning of the war. Then it was not oversimplified and unrealistic to direct all our energies to achieving victory. The point is that where there is a will there is a way; and the government has shown no willingness to achieve the target to which, I say again, we are pledged.
The difficulty in which the government finds itself is that public planning of the character required to meet the target does not suit the private business interests who themselves control the economy to the extent that it is controlled; and it is controlled to a very large

extent. That, of course, is the real explanation of the refusal of the government to adopt the target and the program set out by the United Nations. We say that if this nation could plan to defeat Hitler or could assist in planning the defeat of Hitler-which perhaps is the better way to put it-we could plan equally well for full employment and the maintenance of adequate returns for agriculture in these times of peace.
It is useless to say that so much of our unemployment is seasonal and cannot be otherwise. If we examine the statistics during the war years we find that there was little difference between the numbers of unplaced applicants and persons without jobs in the so-called peak unemployment months-let us say March-and those in the peak of the high employment months, let us say June. As an example, on March 2, 1944, unplaced applicants for work were 68,615. On June 29 of the same year, 1944, the total was 68,773. At the beginning of November of that year, when we are told unemployment should begin to increase because it is seasonal, the total instead of rising had actually fallen to 65,000.
Thus it is clear that if we had a target appealing to this house and to the imagination of the Canadian people we could overcome unemployment and guarantee to everyone able and willing to work a decent opportunity of earning a living.
I have spoken of the seriousness of unemployment as it affects the worker himself and the farmer, but an examination of the dominion bureau of statistics figures on the value of retail trade in Canada teaches us exactly the same lessons. Unemployment and falling farm prices mean a substantial drop in trade in retail stores, particularly in the country stores. It is reflected also in the value of the gross national product at market prices. The dominion bureau of statistics figures record a significant drop in the third quarter of last year over the same quarter in the two preceding years.
When people are unemployed, they are not producing and there is loss in production; and the loss in production through unemployment is greater than the loss from all other causes combined, including sickness, strikes or what you will. Yet according to official estimates and the figures in the 1951 census, Canada is a country which needs many of the things which today are regarded as necessities. We are told that, approximately, Canadian homes need two million furnaces and refrigerators; one and a half million modern toilets and bathrooms; one million washing machines, besides vacuum cleaners, telephones and other modern necessities. I am not including radios and television sets

in those necessities. These are domestic needs. But when we add to these the needs of hundreds of millions of people overseas who could use the products of our farms and our factories, we ask the question, why should anyone in Canada be unemployed?
Our government boasts about the increase in capital investment in our country. I would not minimize the value of this expansion, but as capital development increases employment should rise and our overseas trade should increase. Much of our exports are now in raw materials and partly manufactured products of our forests and our mines. This situation has been brought about largely because of the high level of expenditure on armaments and defence preparations in the United States as well as in other countries.
Over the last number of years we have come to rely more and more on exports of such materials and commodities to our neighbours to the south who-let me remark once again as I have often done in the past-are in many respects competitive to our economy, particularly in the production and marketing of farm commodities. In planning to maintain employment and farm prices we must pay more attention to the trends and financial relationships between Canada and our most reliable overseas customers who are complementary to us rather than competitive with us in these fields.
My opinion is that the government has failed to do this and the mounting unemployment, the falling farm prices, the accumulation of certain farm products, all emphasize the need for a program of intelligent economic planning and trading relationships by the federal government which alone is in a position to undertake it. The failure of the government to meet the needs of such large sections of our Canadian people warrants support of this motion of want of confidence that is before us at the present time.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I do not propose to quote again from the report of the address of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) at the new Reform Club in Quebec on September 19, 1954. I quoted somewhat extensively from it, or rather from newspaper reports of it, on January 10 when I spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. On that occasion the Prime Minister said it was the government's job to find work for all. He went on to say that if the government was not smart enough to organize our economy to provide work for all, it was incompetent. That is our contention today. He invited this house to throw the government out and to put in its place one which could do better 50433-104
Unemployment
if the government failed to do what he said was its job, namely to find employment for all.
The government has failed. Consequently the want of confidence motion is one which should express the opinion of the house-
