-that the government has failed to do the job, or indeed to carry out the pledges and promises made to the people of Canada at the dominion-provincial conference in 1945, or the pledges made when the Prime Minister and the late prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, signed the United Nations charter at San Francisco in 1945.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have all listened with interest to my colleague, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), and to the two members from parties opposite who have already contributed to this debate on unemployment. Understandably, opposition members have placed emphasis on the statistics which indicate an increase in unemployment during the past year. It is true that unemployment in Canada is now at the highest level in our post-war experience, and it is not my intention to minimize in any way the hardship occasioned to some individual Canadians by this situation. It is the concern of the government, as it is of all hon. members, to have unemployment at the absolute minimum consistent with the achievement of the essential goals of our economic life. In considering how these goals are to be achieved, it is, I think, essential that we examine carefully the current economic situation and our future prospects.
By concentrating attention solely or even principally on unemployment figures, and particularly on comparisons of these figures between certain periods, as hon. members opposite have done in this debate, it is possible to leave an impression of the present state of the Canadian economy, which is quite unwarranted. Without minimizing the extent of the temporary slackening in our forward progress which occurred from the end of 1953 through most of 1954, I would like to point out that there are bright spots in the picture as well. It is not my intention to place undue emphasis either on the dark side or on the bright side. What I propose to do is to look at unemployment in relation to other important forces at work in the economy. Such an assessment is, I think, essential to arrive at a sound approach to this problem.
The facts on the extent of current unemployment are available in statistical releases and I will not go over these in detail here. The labour force survey, which

Unemployment
is the one set of statistics available giving a comprehensive and detailed description of Canada's labour force, sets the number of persons without jobs and seeking work at 362,000 this January, compared with 280,000 at the same date last year, and 318,000 at last winter's peak in March. It is important also to note that the number of persons temporarily laid off and also those on short time is about the same as a year ago. Significant also is the fact that the number of persons with jobs, that is, total employment in January and also in the two previous months was about the same or slightly above levels of one year previous. Meanwhile, the labour force has continued to expand, though at a slower rate than population.
In other words, during the past year or so employment has been maintained, but productive activity has not been sufficient to absorb the net increase in persons coming into the labour force.
This levelling off in productive activity was the result of certain new influences which began to affect the market situation in the latter part of 1953 and early 1954. Hon. members are no doubt aware of most of the difficulties encountered-a general business let-down in the United States; a consequent decline during 1954 in Canadian exports to that market; reduced incomes of grain producers, and the effects of this on sales of farm equipment and other manufactured goods; reduced procurement in 1954 of defence goods; a tendency during 1954 for businesses to meet orders from inventories rather than new production; and, finally, intensification of international competition in manufactured goods which presented new difficulties to some manufacturing industries in foreign and also in domestic markets.
In view of these and other problems faced in 1954, the economic achievements of that year have been remarkable indeed. Instead of declining significantly, as might well have been expected, economic activity has remained fairly steady. The gross national product in 1954 was about 2 per cent below the level of the previous year. This decline is fully accounted for by the reduction in grain crops. If crops are excluded, output remained about the same as in the previous year.
As previously indicated, this sustained level of production has not been adequate to absorb the amount of manpower available. Nevertheless, in view of the extent of the adjustments faced, the performance of the economy demonstrates great vigour and resilience. It is, I think, fair to say that it has withstood the threat of the first post-war recession.

Much of the softening in markets in 1954 can be traced in one way or another to a levelling off in the defence build-up in North America and to the subsequent decline in defence procurement. We can be thankful for circumstances which permit the use of less of our resources for defence. Nevertheless, such a development does present a problem of adjustment in that manpower and resources freed from defence and related activities must be absorbed elsewhere. This adjustment has been made more difficult by certain other market fluctuations which are bound to occur from time to time, and which happened to be concentrated in this same period.
From the actual experience in 1954 we can, I think, conclude that this re-absorption process involving the shift of manpower to new activities has been proceeding well. Difficulties of the past year or so have been concentrated to a large extent in certain manufacturing industries. Employment in textiles and in most hard goods industries has declined substantially and in spite of limited improvement in recent months remains well below the levels of a year ago. At the same time, employment in material processing industries, in services and in primary industries such as mining and logging has increased, in some cases quite markedly. The result is that over-all employment has been sustained.
I would like to point out here that Canada has not been alone in encountering increased unemployment. In fact, the business slowdown in the United States commencing in the closing months of 1953 and carrying on into 1954 appears to have been a little more pronounced than that in Canada. In the United States persons out of work and seeking work expressed as a percentage of the labour force increased from an annual average of 2-5 per cent in 1953 to 5 per cent in 1954. In other words, in that country unemployment roughly doubled between the two years. In Canada the corresponding ratios are 2-6 per cent and 4-3 per cent, an increase of about two-thirds.
In recent months, however, there has been a marked improvement in business conditions in the United States. This has been accompanied by a strengthening in the labour market and unemployment in January, 1955, remained below last year's peak. This development is reassuring as regards our own position here in Canada. While unemployment in Canada has not yet shown a corresponding improvement, it is not unusual for changes in business trends here to lag somewhat behind those in the United States. Moreover, with the much greater seasonal

variation experienced in Canada, strengthening forces have much less chance of taking effect during the slack season of the year. For example, promise of a renewed upswing in construction activity is one of the principal stimulating forces in our economy. Yet the extent to which this influence can make itself felt during the winter months is very limited.
Another factor which helps to explain the recent divergence between unemployment trends in the United States and Canada is the contrast in conditions prevailing in the automobile industries of the two countries. In the United States all-out production of automobiles in recent months has been one of the major influences sparking the up-turn in general business activity. In Canada the prolonged strike in Ford plants accentuated the difficulties in manufacturing communities and swelled the numbers of unemployed. I should make it clear that persons on strike are not counted as unemployed. Nevertheless, the widespread effects of the strike on employment in parts plants and in industries affected by loss of income, resulting directly from the strike, were important factors contributing to the level of unemployment reached in January, 1955.
Notwithstanding the current trend of unemployment in Canada, there has been unmistakable evidence of some general strengthening in business conditions in recent months. I have already indicated that national output, excluding crops, was about the same in 1954 as in the preceding year. However, quarterly figures, adjusted for seasonal variation, indicate that over-all output, which turned downward toward the end of 1953, has been increasing since about mid-1954. By the end of that year it appeared to be running about 2 per cent above the level of 1953. This change in direction is reflected in employment figures. Total employment in Canada, after having run a little under previous year levels from December of 1953 to October, 1954, has subsequently been about the same or slightly higher.
These trends suggest that the turning point in the adjustment which I mentioned has already been passed. The important point now to be considered is whether the limited improvement already achieved will gather momentum in the period ahead. A look at prospects in our principal markets should throw some light on this question.
First of all, the export situation. Following a pronounced increase in the period 1949 to 1952, Canada's merchandise exports fell off slightly in 1953. There was a further decline last year of about 6 per cent in value and 3 per cent in volume.
Unemployment
Conditions largely responsible for this decline in exports have already undergone a substantial change for the better. Lower wheat shipments was one of the principal factors in the decline. Hon. members may recall that in the two years ending about mid-1953 the combination of short supplies in overseas countries and bumper crops in Canada boosted our wheat exports to record levels. Between the crop years 1952-53 and 1953-54 wheat and flour exports declined from 386 million bushels to 255 million bushels; still, however, a fairly good record judged by longer-run standards. In recent months a much improved selling atmosphere has developed and sales to date are well ahead of last year. This has not yet been reflected in current exports, as compared with last year, but will gradually become more apparent as the year goes on.
A second reason for lower export totals in 1954 was, of course, the down-turn in the United States economy, even though sales of most of the important export items in that market were reasonably well maintained. This situation is substantially altered as a result of the pick-up now under way in that country. This strengthening coincides with the coming into operation in Canada of extensive new capacity for the production of industrial materials such as aluminum and iron ore. Consequently, we can reasonably look forward to a better year as regards trade with the United States.
Export prospects in overseas markets are also favourable. The situation in overseas countries was, in fact, one of the bright spots in the trade position during 1954. Except for the special circumstances relating to wheat, sales to the United Kingdom, western Europe and a number of other countries were substantially higher last year. This reflects the growing economic strength of these countries.
The present prosperity in western Europe has been associated with a substantial rise in output during the past two years. This reflects important progress on the part of European countries in overcoming the fundamental post-war imbalance between domestic requirements and production levels. In addition, hard currency reserves of the nondollar area have been rising, permitting a general relaxation of restrictions against dollar goods. The United Kingdom has removed discriminatory restrictions against nearly all bulk materials, such as grains, wood products and metals, which are of primary importance to Canada. There has been a better market in the United Kingdom for Canadian agricultural and food products, such as tobacco, salmon and apples, some

Unemployment
of which are again moving in volume across the Atlantic. This move toward fewer import controls has been followed by both European and commonwealth countries. South Africa and Belgium have been added to the list of countries which have effectively ceased to discriminate against dollar imports. Following the commonwealth meetings in January, 1954, both Australia and New Zealand increased their allocations for the purchase of goods from the dollar area, resulting in greater sales of a fairly wide range of Canadian products, including limited quantities of manufactured goods.
The recent improvement in conditions in foreign markets is already being reflected in better export figures, which in volume terms are running at peacetime record levels for this period of the year. A noticeable improvement first became apparent in November of 1954, when exports increased 4 per cent over the same month in 1953. This increase widened to 8 per cent in December and to 17 per cent in January, the latest month for which figures are available. In value terms sales for these three months are still a little below the levels reached two and three years ago. However, price levels are also lower. Consequently, in volume terms our exports in this period reached the highest level ever recorded for these winter months, in peacetime.
In January, 1955, exports amounted to $310 million, 17 per cent above the same month of 1954. The increase is about equally divided between sales to the United Kingdom and sales to the United States. Sales to the United Kingdom have been substantially higher for some months. However, this is the first significant increase in the value of exports to the United States in more than a year and is no doubt associated with the improvement in business activity in that country.
All in all, there is good reason to expect this firmer trend in exports to continue. This, in turn, will have a marked effect on employment during the coming year.
Having looked at past performance and present prospects in the export field, let us now turn to the domestic situation. What is the outlook for capital investment? I am glad to report that the information now available on expansion plans for 1955 is reassuring indeed.
Capital expenditures in 1954 turned out to be down by about 5 per cent from the 1953 level and were, in fact, lower than the intentions reported earlier in the year. This short-fall seems to have been the result of

certain retarding factors such as unfavourable weather during the construction season and a poor harvest. There was no indication, however, of cancellation of major expansion plans. To some extent, therefore, the shortfall in 1954 programs means simply a larger carryover into the current year.
The brief duration and relative mildness of the recession in the United States is undoubtedly reassuring to businessmen who are considering capital expansion at this time. This newly inspired confidence in the United States economy, together with the improvement in international trade, come at a crucial time in Canada's development. With much of the post-war re-equipment now completed, and with manufacturing industries facing stiffer international competition, future expansion in Canada may depend to a greater degree than in recent years upon a sound international trading position.
At any rate, the results of this year's survey of investment intentions which are contained in the report "Private and Public Investment in Canada-Outlook 1955", tabled a few days ago, point to an immediate resumption of an upward trend in capital spending in Canada. The survey indicates that over-all capital expenditures of $5-8 billion are anticipated in Canada for 1955. This figure is nearly 6 per cent above actual expenditure of $5'5 billion last year. The estimate includes all planned expenditures in Canada for new capital facilities and covers expenditures for new construction and for machinery and equipment made by business groups, institutions and governments as well as estimated expenditures for new housing. Looking at the major changes by industrial groups, the sharpest increases are indicated for mining, institutional building and housing. Outlays by the trade, finance, and commercial service groups, and by government bodies are expected to increase moderately, while capital spending in agriculture and in utilities is likely to remain about the same as in 1954.
An encouraging feature of this year's survey is the moderate rise in anticipated capital outlays in manufacturing industries. This reverses a downward trend in evidence for some time past. These increases in capital expenditures are mainly concentrated in material processing industries such as paper products, chemicals and non-ferrous metal products. On the other hand, in a number of manufacturing industries capital spending plans appear to reflect the continuing market difficulties being encountered as a result of intensified competition on an international scale. However, even in those industries

most affected, outlays for new capital goods, though reduced, remain sizeable.
Further details concerning the nature and composition of this year's investment plans can be obtained from the published report. I would, however, like to lay particular emphasis on two important implications of the projected rise in capital outlays.
In the first place, it illustrates clearly and forcibly the confidence with which Canadian business, collectively, views the nation's long-run economic future. Even in the face of the substantial additions to capacity since world war II, the business community is continuing to add to its capital facilities at an undiminished rate. This can only mean that businessmen anticipate not only sustained markets but growing markets for years to come.
Next, let us look at the consumer market, which, it should be remembered, accounts for by far the larger portion of goods and services produced and sold in Canada.
First of all, it is important to note that personal spending during 1954 continued to rise. In fact, it was the Canadian consumer who was largely responsible for holding national activity at a fairly even pace in the face of moderate declines in both exports and capital expenditure. In 1954 consumer expenditures amounted to approximately $15 6 billion, nearly 3 per cent above the level of 1953. Canada's population was up 2-7 per cent between the same two years, indicating that on a per capita basis consumer expenditure has been well maintained. Now this is another remarkable achievement for a period in which we have faced substantial difficulties. In spite of the adjustments which the economy has had to contend with, Canadians have, on the average, been able to maintain the high standard of living achieved during the preceding unusually prosperous years.
This high level of consumer outlays was supported by sustained personal incomes. Notwithstanding the increase in unemployment, wage and salary payments rose by about 2 per cent in 1954 compared with the previous year. Workers were able to earn this higher income even though the average working week was a little shorter. Also in 1954 Canadians received about 10 per cent more in interest, dividends and net rental incomes and in social security payments from governments. The latter reflected a greater volume of family allowance and old age security payments as well as unemployment insurance benefits. Rising incomes in these sectors offset in aggregate the decline in net farm income so that total personal income was at about the same high level as in the previous year. After deducting
Unemployment
direct personal tax payments, income left at the disposal of individuals was at least as high as in 1953.
These, in brief, were the circumstances affecting the Canadian consumer market in 1954. Looking ahead, prospects of increased activity in both capital goods and export industries should, in turn, bolster income positions. Consequently, consumer demand, which remained firm in 1954, may be even better in the coming year.
In view of the circumstances I have described, it is reasonable to anticipate continued firming in both foreign and domestic markets. As previously indicated, production trends have already shown some response to these strengthening influences. Over-all output is now running a little ahead of a year ago. However, with increasing effectiveness in the use of manpower, this rise in output has been achieved with, as yet, scarcely no increase in employment. With a continuing rise in the labour force, unemployment is still running somewhat higher than a year ago.
It is to be realized, however, that the strength now in evidence in investment and export markets has not yet had its full impact on conditions generally and cannot be expected to do so during the slack season of the year. As the year draws on we can, I am confident, look forward to a broader resumption of expansionary trends with an accompanying growth in job opportunities.
If these are the economic prospects ahead of us, what role should the government play? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that what is needed is a continuation of the sensible economic policies which have enabled Canadians to enjoy a lengthy post-war period of economic expansion and improvement in earning opportunities and living standards. These policies are directed towards creating a favourable economic climate in which individual initiative thrives, and businessmen are encouraged to expand their capital facilities in order to cater to growing domestic and foreign markets.
Some hon. members of the opposition have been saying that the government has stood idly by and watched the number of unemployed rise. Nothing could be further from the truth as the economic achievements of 1954 so well demonstrate. I do not want to claim that the economic policies which were followed were solely or mainly responsible for the reasonably good showing in 1954. Obviously and unquestionably the dominating factors were the continuation of basic forces of sound economic growth and the initiative,

Unemployment
energy and good judgment of the Canadian people in all walks of life. But what I am suggesting is that the economic policies that have been followed have facilitated the adjustment processes which we experienced in Canada last year. The effects of the adjustment were minimized for most Canadians.
Here is a brief summary of the economic policies that have been pursued. I will not go into any details, but I can say that each and every one of these helped Canadians to find jobs and thus earn more money to spend on t'he things they wanted to buy, or to build houses, or to expand business capital facilities, or to sell more abroad.
1.	Tax collections have been lower, and for the first time since 1946 a net budgetary deficit is indicated. Even though incomes of most Canadians rose, the personal income tax take has been reduced, a drop of 2 per cent during 1954, as compared with the year previous. Sales and excise tax collections were also down 5 per cent, though total domestic sales, as I mentioned, remained firm.
2.	Monetary conditions eased considerably in the latter part of 1953 and the early part of 1954, and again even more recently. This has made it possible for provincial and municipal governments, as well as businesses and other private borrowers in the investment market, to raise money for capital expenditures more readily and at lower rates of interest. It has also ensured that there was ample supply of bank credit available to finance worthwhile and constructive undertakings.
3.	The new National Housing Act, 1954, made it easier for people to build houses by reducing down payments and lengthening the period of amortization. At the same time the availability of mortgage credit was broadened considerably through the entry of the chartered banks and the Quebec savings banks into the field. The interest rate on National Housing Act loans was reduced.
4.	In foreign trade our earnest and unremitting efforts brought some results, partly reflected in an increase in many of our overseas sales, partly in persuading our friends to the south to go slow with some of their restrictive measures in the interest of greater international commercial stability. The medium of export credit insurance was used increasingly during 1954 to reduce the risks Canadian businessmen faced in doing business abroad. Policies written for the 12-month period ended September, 1954, amounted to $35 million, or some 40 per cent above the corresponding period a year before. Much of the additional export credit was for the

medium term and covered largely capital goods, especially farm machinery and equipment.
5.	Personal incomes and consequent consumer spending were bolstered by increases of about 10 per cent in the volume of social security benefits, as I mentioned earlier. A further increase in such payments is in sight for this year. The program of allowances for totally and permanently disabled persons, passed by parliament during the last session, has come into effect in a number of provinces as of the 1st of January this year. Further, as announced in the speech from the throne, the program of allowances for the blind is again being expanded by providing wider coverage and scope of benefits.
6.	In agriculture, orderly marketing, particularly in wheat, helped to tide us over a difficult market situation, assuring farmers of as good returns as appeared possible under the circumstances. Price support continued to help farmers with respect to such important commodities as butter and eggs. Apple growers in Nova Scotia who suffered grievously from storm damage received financial assistance.
7.	In fishing, a number of steps were taken to assist the industry in finding new markets abroad, in providing aid to modernize fishing fleets and equipment, to find new fishing grounds, to develop more scientific methods of operation for fish processing.
8.	Several of our mining industries continued to have difficulties, particularly coal and gold. Substantial financial assistance was provided to those industries.
9.	The tightened anti-dumping regulations enacted in the last session of parliament have helped a number of our domestic manufacturing industries.
10.	To help the unemployed, particularly during the winter months, the Unemployment Insurance Act was amended earlier this session to provide for an increase in the duration and scale of supplementary benefits. A major revision of this act is proposed during the present session. The local offices of the national employment service have speeded up their activities to bring men and jobs together.
11.	Defence expenditures during the year past have been running at a somewhat lower level. I shall make a report about the progress of our defence procurement program later on in the session. All I want to say now is that the decline was more than offset by rising civilian expenditures, particularly those of the social security type and the public investment type. For example, expenditures of the Department of Public Works

during 1954 were 35 per cent above those of 1953 and expenditures of the Department of Transport during 1954 were 14 per cent above those of 1953. Several major projects were completed or were nearing completion, such as the Canso causeway, and railway extensions to Lynn Lake and to Kitimat. Major new projects initiated last year included the St. Lawrence seaway, the $30 million military camp and housing project at Gagetown, New Brunswick, and access railway lines to open up newly-discovered mineral deposits in the Chibougamau area in Quebec and the Hills-port region in Ontario. In addition there were dozens of smaller projects undertaken of particular importance to the development and service of our country, ranging all the way from the Yarmouth ferry terminal to the dredging of the First Narrows at Vancouver. Provincial governments were approached to speed up the construction of the trans-Canada highway to which the Canadian government contributes 50 per cent of the cost.
For the fiscal year 1955-56 total federal funds available for new construction work including advances to public bodies such as the St. Lawrence seaway authority amount to $435 million, which is approximately $100 million higher than the value of work being carried out in 1954-55. I suggest to the leader of the C.C.F. party that he is quite mistaken in saying that there is no additional works program under way.
Many hon. members seem to believe that the answer to unemployment lies in the volume of federal public works. In my opinion this is entirely fallacious. Our difficulty in Canada is seasonal unemployment, or in other words the problem of maintaining a high level of employment in the winter months. Excepting inland navigation and the shore jobs incidental thereto, construction work is perhaps of all occupations the one least capable of maintaining full employment over the full twelve months. Many types of public works involving large expenditures are comparatively small employers of labour. For example, I am told that the more than $20 million expenditure in the Canso causeway provided peak employment for about 250 men.
Nevertheless, we will admit at once that the volume of construction work is important to the men normally employed in construction, but I will point out that unless continuing employment beyond the construction period is involved, it is of little importance to other classes of workers.
Obviously it will be of no great help to the women in the textile trades or to the men formerly employed on the assembly lines of the agricultural implement industry.
Unemployment
The fact that construction work was the government's solution to unemployment in the depression of the early thirties probably affects present thinking. Then 25 cents an hour and a pick and shovel job on highway work was considered a complete solution. Today that kind of relief work would be of little value.
A high level of employment in the Canadian economy can only be achieved by a program that will lift the Canadian economy as a whole to an extent that suitable employment for all types of workers can be made available. That is the program on which the government is engaged. The fact that the program is producing results will, I think, be made apparent to all during the next three or four months.
In expanding our public investment program this year the government has selected a number of useful projects which will contribute to the long-term development of our country. To add to this some hastily-conceived make-work projects, it seems to me, would be an unwise use of public funds. In saying this I am not denying that there are a number of constructive development works which the government can undertake. A good many such projects of major importance have been undertaken or are under way as, for example, the St. Lawrence seaway and railway extensions to the north country. Such projects help the long-term development of our country and stimulate the expansion of business. I am sure there will be ample opportunities to undertake similar useful projects in the future.
In summing up, I might say that we on this side of the house do not look at public investment as a panacea for solving all our unemployment problems. Increased public investment spending if applied judiciously and timed right can help, but it is only one of the economic policies designed to aid in the maintenance of a high level of employment and income. There are many other economic policies that should be followed and, in fact, are being followed by the government in dealing with problems of economic adjustment we must inevitably face in Canada from time to time.
I, for one, believe that the Canadian economy remains basically healthy and continues to expand, despite an occasional interruption. In my opinion this is no time to lose sight of our larger objectives or to permit our confidence to be unduly shaken by fears which are not justified by the facts. The present level of unemployment is the result of known factors, which I have briefly attempted to outline. Knowledge of the causes has permitted us to act effectively within the proper sphere of governmental

Unemployment
activities to meet the situation as it has developed. I have briefly described some of the steps we have taken. The full results desired cannot be achieved immediately, as economic factors must be given time to operate. However, some success is already apparent. The time may come when there has to be greater emphasis on supplementary measures to maintain employment and incomes. If this does become necessary we must ensure that these supplementary measures support and do not interfere with the attainment of a highly productive low-cost efficient economy.

Mr. Speaker, I think the house generally will recognize that the government now has come to the conclusion that this, unemployment problem is becoming serious. I think that is evident, because in the four speeches that have been given so far we have had two by leading cabinet ministers who gave prepared speeches on the subject.
As we listened to those speeches I hope I am correct when I say that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) appeared to be sympathetic toward the position in which the unemployed find themselves. But he said as a sort of consolation, "Oh, well, things are not much worse than they were a year ago, because we had 500,000 unemployed then and have only 600,000 now; that is nothing to be too excited about." But his sympathies were there.
Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) came along and told us that he was not going to minimize the importance of unemployment or the position in which these people find themselves, but he went on to say, "What should the government do about it?" He said this, "We should continue along the same lines; we should do about the same thing as we have been doing, and if the time comes when we should really take this thing seriously then the government will have to bring forth some other remedial measures." I am sure that will not be much consolation to the 600,000 unemployed people who are looking to the government for some remedy.
I do not think anyone would say that the government is not concerned with the present situation with regard to unemployment. It will be recalled that in the speech from the throne the government had a line or two about unemployment. They said at that time that unemployment was of a regional and seasonal nature, that that was what was being experienced. The Minister of Trade and Commerce reiterated tonight that it was mostly seasonal, and that he hoped as time went on it would correct itself. On

February 25 the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said that the government very seriously regretted the developing unemployment across the country. So I think we can take it that the government is concerned about this matter.
But that is not going to be good enough for the 600,000 people who are unemployed. Everybody across the country knows that something must be done about it. Even the Conservative party in this house has shown some little concern, because they have put forth an amendment. I was somewhat interested in their amendment. Let me put it on the record:
in the opinion of this house, because of the grave state of unemployment in Canada as disclosed by the joint statement of the Department of Labour and the dominion bureau of statistics on February 23rd last, the government should immediately give consideration to the formulation of plans to deal with this emergency, and to the necessary steps to establish a long-term program for expanding employment to be presented to parliament during the present session.
So they are concerned. I had my pencil and paper ready to jot down what their cure was going to be, but they very skilfully avoided any mention of what they were going to suggest to cure this unemployment problem. I think we can take it that when they presented their amendment they were saying to themselves, "This is not our problem. We have no policy to correct this unemployment, so let the government worry about it."
I think that is very true. As we look back in history we find that the Conservative party was in power for a period of time during the thirties when we had unemployment, and they certainly did not do anything about it. The Liberals were in power; they started unemployment rolling, but they did not do anything to stop it. They came back in 1935, and they did not do anything about it. History has shown that the only cure for unemployment that has ever come about under our present orthodox system during the leadership by the Conservatives or Liberals in this country is war or preparation for war.
I am not suggesting for one moment that the present government would wish a continuation of war or preparation for war in order to solve our unemployment problem, but the hard fact is that they have no other cure for it. It is not good enough to say, "Oh, well, the construction program, when it gets really under way"-and it has been under way now for several years-"is going to cure the unemployment problem". It is going to do no such thing. Let us therefore make no mistake about it. This unemployment affair is becoming a serious problem. Everyone in this country recognizes it to be so.

I want just to show you how concerned the people of Canada are with regard to this matter, and how they are looking to us here in this house and particularly to the government to come forward with some solution to this problem. When the municipalities and the provinces are appealing to this government to bring forth some program in order to solve this problem, it is indeed serious. 1 have in my hand an extract from the Ottawa Citizen of February 25. The heading of the article is " 'More Jobs' Cry Grows" and it reads in part as follows:
Toronto Mayor Nathan Phillips and a civic delegation pleaded with the federal government today for remedial measures to halt the "demoralization, want and discontentment" of spreading unemployment.
The group met a cabinet group composed of Trade Minister Howe, Finance Minister Harris, Works Minister Winters and Labour Minister Gregg following an undertaking by the government in the Commons yesterday to stage a full-dress debate on unemployment, probably Monday.
Then down further:
The Toronto group said these statistics and the "stark realities" facing those in authority in the larger cities especially "compels everyone responsible for leadership in government to assess the avenues of possible remedial measures".
They are looking to us to do something. I am sure they are going to search in vain when they go through the speeches made here in the house tonight by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In them they are going to find little hope for a solution of their problems.
Then the Ontario welfare council, which keeps a close eye on this matter, has come to the conclusion that something must be done.
I am not going to read this whole brief to you, Mr. Speaker; I am just going to quote one little section of it in order to show what a similarity there is between the present situation and that of the 1930's. On page 2 of their brief they say this:
At our meeting, the administrator of one hostel which serves "single men", and among them many transients, reported that he had registered 3,200 such men in the past three months. He reported that they had come from all parts of Canada-
That is not regional, sir; from all parts of Canada.
-and for many of them the only help which could be provided by a private agency was food and shelter for a minimum period-and a request that they move on. In one instance, four such men were arrested on a theft charge within a few hours of being "pushed on".
How familiar that phrase is, when we remember that in the hungry thirties men went to these municipalities in search of relief and could not find it, then were told, "Here is a meal; now move on". Then when they hopped the train to find another job in
Unemployment
another place they were arrested as vagabonds. Here we find this same thing. So I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that when these labour organizations read the speeches that were made here tonight they are going to find little consolation indeed; and this in a country so wealthy as Canada.
Tell us what you want done about it.
I am coming to you in a minute.
Tell us that in one, two, three order.

I am coming to that. I am going to read only one line from the brief of the Canadian Welfare Council, but I say to you that in a land so abundantly blessed with natural resources and having such a tremendous productive capacity there is no excuse for want or poverty in this day and age. On the second page of their brief there is just one line that I want to read. It is as follows:
Much of the distress and suffering referred to above is unnecessary and could be prevented.
I agree with that statement wholeheartedly. This problem is serious, Mr. Speaker, and it is continuing to grow. Figures have been put on the record, and I also want to put a few figures on it. I think possibly I have about the latest figures, because this information was sent over to me from the dominion bureau of statistics just on Friday, February 25. In this review the figure with regard to applications for employment on file at N.E.S. offices on January 22, 1955 is given as 570,000, and for persons without jobs and seeking work from L.F. survey, the figure given is 362,000. If we take the figure of 570,000- and that is fairly close now to 600,000, if it does not go over that figure-that is an increase of 206,000 since December 9. That is a tremendous increase in unemployment. It is all very well for the ministers to stand up here on the floor of the house and say in effect to the unemployed who are looking to them for a solution, "Just keep going; hang on; do without a few more meals for the next two or three weeks and things will finally solve themselves". That is not good enough.
They never said any such thing.

Let my hon. friend read the minister's speech in Hansard. If he does so, he will find that in essence that is what he said.
In my statement here the other day when I said that the total number of unemployed now was almost equal to that in the 1930's

somebody said, "Oh, nonsense". I have the return sent over from the dominion bureau of statistics for 1931-1950. I turn to page 15 and I go to the year 1931. I find that the number of persons without jobs and seeking work then was 475,000; in 1932 the number was 733,000; and in 1933-and that was the peak year-it was 817,000. We have almost 600,000 now. Those are only the unemployed registered by the national employment service. It is generally conceded that if you take 20 or 25 per cent more than that you would come close to those who are not registered. Thus you would have well over 800,000. ,
Nonsense.

You just figure it out and see. Just a moment ago I read from the brief of the welfare council an extract that points out that conditions are almost the same. It is indeed a serious problem for those who are unemployed and have families to keep. Mind you, the 600,000 that is being spoken of does not include members of the families. The number going hungry now would therefore be much more than 600,000. A moment ago I was asked to say what we would do. I shall come to that shortly.
We have heard the socialists in this house claim that the greatest difficulty we are facing now is as the result of private enterprise, and that what we need is the socializing of everything and long-term planning. Private enterprise is being blamed for the difficulty in which we find ourselves today. They say that what we need is more jobs and that private enterprise has failed to give those jobs.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that nothing could be further from the truth. Private enterprise has produced so many goods that there is now a surplus and as a consequence men are laid off. Literally they have produced themselves out of jobs. The goods are there. There is no fault on the part of private enterprise. It has really exceeded itself. The difficulty is that there is something lacking in connection with the distribution of those goods.
In a debate like this, Mr. Speaker, some of the socialists particularly like to blame private enterprise. They supposedly sponsor the workers of this country, giving the impression across the country that the workers are all socialists. Again nothing could be further from the truth, because the workers' organizations and the workers generally are not socialist-minded. Let me repeat here a statement made by William Green, president of

the American Federation of Labor, as reported in the Wholesale Grocers' News of October, 1943. He said:
As the spokesman for a labour organization with 61 million members, I want to make it emphatically clear here and now that the American Federation of Labor stands foursquare in support of free and private enterprise. We recognize the right to own and manage property for public service and private profit. We will oppose any attempt to abridge, restrict or interfere with the functions of free enterprise.
He continues along the same line. Here in Canada Mr. Percy Bengough used almost the same words, only he went further and dissociated himself from any political organization whatever. So when we are discussing a matter of this importance we should never attribute socialism as a part of labour's program.
Let me turn to some of the responsibilities of the government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said a while ago: Now, what should the government do? He went on and said in effect that we should continue along the same lines that we are following. Both he and the Minister of Labour said very definitely, and I think rightly, that it was not the duty of the government to supply jobs, that that was a part of private enterprise. Private enterprise has done so.
No.

The hon. member for Spadina says "no", that that is not true. Let the Minister of Labour get up and correct me if I am wrong when I say it is his view that the government is not necessarily bound to supply jobs, but that it is the part of private enterprise. I do not think he will stand up and say that, even in support of the hon. member for Spadina. Certainly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) will never get up and support him, so I do not think the hon. member is going to have much support for that view. I believe it is the business of private enterprise to produce jobs, and they will do so if they are given the opportunity without government interference.
I said a moment ago that the Minister of Finance certainly would not support a suggestion such as that put forward by the hon. member for Spadina. Let me refer to what he has said, as found in the Montreal Gazette of Friday, February 25. He is reported as saying:
In this country it is still left mainly to the private business world to plan expansion and development, to supply capital for new ventures, assume financial risks and take the initiative in all the ways that provide employment and careers for those who work for salary and wages. This fact should never be lost sight of.

You could not get it clearer than that, and there it is. But, Mr. Speaker, when we find the federal government doing anything, especially as a matter of policy, that interferes with private enterprise and so affects the earning power of the people or, as it is sometimes called, the purchasing power of the people, it is increasing the problem of unemployment; and when the government so interfere they should accept their responsibility and face up to the issue. When we find unemployment increasing as the result of government policy, then it is the responsibility of the federal government to do something and not do as they have done tonight, merely shrug it off and say, "We will wait until the thing gets a little bit worse before we do anything because, after all, it is not too bad."
Let me give an illustration of what I mean. When the province of Alberta was endeavouring to develop its gas resources and wanted to export gas to the best and most logical market, the United States, the federal government said no, sir, you cannot do that. A policy was established then by this Liberal government that the gas should go to eastern Canada by an all-Canadian line whether or not that line was economically feasible. The man who did that, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, was the very man who, when the oil pipe line was built, had it constructed in the most economical way, namely, by having it go through the United States.
As the result of that interference, what has happened? The government is now considering the possibility of having to subsidize private enterprise because of a mistaken government policy. The delay they have caused has meant that the people of Alberta and Canada generally have lost billions of dollars that would have been of great assistance in this time of need. So I say that when the government, through their policy, interfere with private enterprise and prevent it from doing the very thing that the Minister of Finance says it should do, it is the responsibility of the government to step in and do something and not merely sit back and say that they will go along and do the same as they have been doing before.
Another place where the federal government has interfered with private enterprise is in the British Columbia dam development. There again they have-
You said all that last week.
-prevented the British Columbia government from going ahead and developing the project there in the interests of the people of that province.

Surely you are not going to start another filibuster.
Unemployment

Let me give another example referred to tonight by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The government have failed to establish a national fuel policy for Canada, and as a result they are ruining one of the greatest industries in this country, the coal mining industry. Our mines are being closed, but at the same time we allow United States interests to ship many millions of tons more coal into this country than we produce. There again is government interference, and something should be done. I think the government should carry on a very extensive public works program at this time because of their unwarranted interference with private enterprise.
In the next ten minutes you tell us what you are going to do.

It cannot be said that private enterprise does not do the job if it is given the opportunity to do it. As I said a moment ago, private enterprise has produced the goods and has paid good wages, but another thing the matter is that the federal government has confiscated most of the wages through taxation. If there were a lowering of taxation that too would be of some assistance, and I quote as my witness to that the Minister of Finance. He seems to be the only one who is realistic about these problems. As found in the Montreal Gazette of February 25 there is the following:
H?,r,ris said in a speech in Montreal last November:	I confess myself concerned about tax
rates under which the government takes away half or more of the rewards of hard work which leads to promotion."	wmcn
It is about time the government did something, and not merely sat back on their haunches and said that the situation is not so much worse than it was a year ago, so there is not much to be concerned about. By so doing they have confessed their utter failure to cope with the problem of unemployment.
What have the Liberals done? They have been carrying on the same policy that they have carried on ever since there has been a Liberal party. That policy brought on the depression of the 1930's, a depression that was only cured by war or preparation for war. We come now, some years after the war, to a time when there are 600,000 people unemployed, and the numbers are still climbing.
Then I come to the Conservatives who moved an amendment this afternoon. What have they done? What did they do? Nothing different. They have nothing new to offer, and so the people of Canada are disregarding them as the official opposition because they realize that the Conservatives are not an

Unemployment
opposition and that some other party is going to have to take their place if we ever expect to have-
What is your policy?

Now you just wait; you are going to get it. We at least are going to do more than the Conservatives. We are going to tell you how this thing can be cured. We may be wrong but under a democracy we have a right to be wrong, and that is something a socialist can never understand. But we are convinced that our policy will give the desired results.
Go right ahead.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The right to be wrong is your fundamental freedom.
That is a function of democracy. Of course I would not expect you socialists to recognize it.
Give us your policy, one, two, three.
The Conservatives do not even have anything to offer, right or wrong.
No right to be wrong.
They have so little that they joined Social Credit.

The government can increase public works but that is not going to be sufficient, and they are going to find that out. They will have to encourage private enterprise to take care of this job. I have heard some of my socialist friends here say, what about your program? I want to refer to the socialists before I say what Social Credit will do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is five minutes to ten.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us have a look at the socialists.
Your time is almost up.
There is only one country in the world in which socialism is practised where they have full employment, and that is Russia.
Oh, nonsense.
Didn't you know that before?
You said that you had the freedom to be wrong.
They have full employment because of war and preparation for war. If we refer to New Zealand we will find it too had a socialist government. It failed and the people kicked it out.
What about Sweden?
Do not class Sweden as being socialists of your type.
What about Norway?

What about Australia? They had a socialist government which failed miserably and was kicked out. Then England a few years ago had a socialist government. We used to hear about what the socialist government in England was doing. Well, it proved to be a miserable failure.
Did it?

Yes, and it was
kicked out. Private enterprise put the country back on its feet.
Churchill hung on to everything they did.

Let us come a little bit closer to home. Let us take the province of Saskatchewan as an example. What has the socialist government done in Saskatchewan? Well, Mr. Speaker, anything that Saskatchewan has was achieved by the efforts of private enterprise.
Nonsense.
Let us just take a look at it. Just wait. I am talking to you now and I want you to listen.
What about automobile insurance?

Let us take a look at oil in Saskatchewan. One of the greatest prospects for prosperity in Saskatchewan is in the development of oil, but what did their minister say in that regard? He said that any government which would take its own money to develop its oil resources would soon face bankruptcy. What did they do then? They went over to Alberta, and we showed them how to do the job. They went back and copied us, and now they are having some success in that field. That is private enterprise.
What are you going to do about unemployment?

Private enterprise, Mr. Speaker. Again let us refer to the Saskatchewan socialist government. What about agriculture? Would any of my friends who are sitting on my immediate right say that agriculture is socialistic? That is one thing they do not like to say. Mind you, one or two of them have gone on record in this house as saying they would even socialize agriculture, so let them not say they would not socialize agriculture if they got the opportunity. I am pointing out that one of the

greatest sources of revenue of the province of Saskatchewan is its agriculture, a private enterprise. Then, Mr. Speaker-
Tell us about Alberta oil.
-Saskatchewan gets a great deal of its money from family allowances. That too is derived directly or indirectly from the benefits of private enterprise.
Socialist legislation.

That is one thing this government did for which I think they deserve a great deal of credit, and it is my belief that it is one of the things which is cushioning the effects of unemployment. If it were not for family allowances and the payment of unemployment insurance and increased supplementary benefits we would find the situation much graver than it is now. However, that is not sufficient grounds for the government to say we will sit back and they will take care of our problem.
Let us go back to the socialists in Saskatchewan and discuss these people who condemn private enterprise every time they stand on their feet. Look at the millions of dollars, Mr. Speaker, that the socialists in the province of Saskatchewan have got from P.F.A.; and that too is a result of the achievements of private enterprise.
The farmers paid for it.
Oh, Mr. Speaker, those people who condemn private enterprise and are so ready to stand on their feet to condemn it; look at them.
At least we do not stand on our heads, like some other people do.

Mr. Speaker, some of the wealthiest men in this House of Commons are socialists, and they have made their money from private enterprise. We have some farmers who are socialists. Some have the finest farms stocked with pure-bred cattle. This too is private enterprise. Some of them own large areas of timber and have sawmills on their property; private enterprise again. Then those same members have the audacity to stand up in this house and condemn the very hand which is feeding them.
The Tories are still with you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You have one minute in which to tell us what you are going to do.

No, I have more than one minute in which to tell you what I am going to do. Although it is close to
Unemployment
ten o'clock I still have 15 minutes, and I intend to take my full time in this matter because this question of unemployment is so serious.
You are not talking about that.
Oh, yes, I am. I am talking about where the cure for unemployment will be found, and it is not going to be through socialism. The records will show that. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to again'-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Give a good minute's worth.
-if I have another minute or two-*
Tell us, one, two, three.

In Saskatchewan and these other places socialism has been a failure. Let us take a quick look at those places where Social Credit governments have been in power. Take the province of Alberta. We started in 1935 from nothing at all.
The oil companies took it.
We have risen now to become one of the most prosperous provinces in Canada. That is recognized by everyone.
Oil.

It does not make any difference whether it is oil or what it is. We have done it through the efforts of private enterprise. Then there is British Columbia coming right along in the development of her natural resources, in following the principles of Social Credit.
Oh, oh.
They are going to be the second province in Canada that has made such great achievements.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He has not told us anything yet.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Johnston (Bow River) moves, seconded by Mr. Quelch, that the debate be now adjourned.
Go ahead.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Some hon. members say "Go ahead". I heard the hon. member for Bow River state that he had 15 minutes more and that he intended to take them all. Is it the wish of the hon. member to conclude his speech this evening?
I should like to call it ten o'clock.

Go on, answer tonight.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He needs time to think it over.

Give us the answer tomorrow.
On motion of Mr. Johnston (Bow River) the debate was adjourned.

Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that in view of the importance of this issue we might proceed with this tomorrow by unanimous consent. I think I speak on behalf of the official opposition in saying this, and if the other opposition parties would agree I would suggest that the government might welcome the opportunity to proceed with it tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, I think the importance of this topic is such that I suggest we continue the discussion as soon as we can. I think the public will expect us to complete this debate and endeavour to find some solution to the unemployment problem. I would suggest we continue the debate, if it is agreeable to the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If the leader of the house is considering this suggestion, we would like to hear what he has to say. I hope he has in mind that if any change is made, the same number of private members' days will be retained as he had planned to give to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with his usual wisdom the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has put his finger on the problem.
You mean he upset the applecart.
The applejack.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was the intention of the government that tomorrow and a week from tomorrow would be the remaining private members' days. We would like to have priority after a week from tomorrow. If hon. members wish to give up tomorrow to continue this debate we shall be glad to do so.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
